intro.heading: The Middle Years Programme is marked on criteria, not on content
paragraphs: Parents in Karama whose child moves from a British or Indian-curriculum school into an MYP school usually arrive with the same confusion. The report has no percentages. It has a number between one and seven for each subject, and underneath it four letters, each with a number between zero and eight. Nobody has explained what those letters mean, the child says the teacher marked them on criterion C, and the natural response is to buy a tutor who will teach more content. That is frequently the wrong purchase.

The MYP assesses four criteria in every subject, each scored from zero to eight against published descriptors. In sciences they are knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. In mathematics they are knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. In language and literature they are analysing, organising, producing text, and using language. The four levels are then combined and converted to a grade from one to seven using published grade boundaries.

The consequence is that a student can know a great deal and still score a four, because the criterion being assessed was not knowledge. A mathematics task marked on investigating patterns rewards generalising a rule and justifying it; a student who computes every case correctly and never states a general rule has answered a different question. A sciences task marked on processing and evaluating rewards handling data and identifying limitations; a student who writes a beautiful explanation of the theory has not addressed the criterion at all.

Alongside the criteria sits a document most parents have never seen and every student is given: the task-specific clarification. For each assessed task the teacher rewrites the generic descriptors in the language of that task, which means the exact requirements for the top level are written down in advance. Reading it before starting the work is the single highest-return habit in the MYP, and a startling number of students in this belt have never been shown how.

The other things that matter in the MYP are approaches to learning skills, which are taught explicitly and assessed implicitly, interdisciplinary units that combine two subject groups and are marked on their own criteria, service as action, and in MYP 5 the Personal Project. The Personal Project is the component families worry about most and leave latest, and it is marked on its own small set of criteria rather than on the quality of the object the student produced.

What follows is the structure, the conversion, where levels are actually lost, the Personal Project, and the real gaps on the way into the Diploma. Lessons are delivered one to one, live online. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we offer only in India.

programmes.name: MYP years 1 to 3
programmes.description: The eight subject groups taught broadly, with criteria applied at an earlier level of demand. This is where habits are formed: reading the task-specific clarification, structuring an investigation, communicating mathematics in full sentences and diagrams, and reflecting in a way that goes beyond saying the work went well. Students who build those habits early find MYP 4 and 5 much less turbulent.

programmes.name: MYP years 4 and 5
programmes.description: Subject choice narrows, mathematics divides into standard and extended, and the demand of the criterion descriptors rises sharply. MYP 5 carries the Personal Project and, in schools that offer it, the option of MYP eAssessment through on-screen examinations and ePortfolios leading to the MYP Certificate. This is the stage where the gap to Diploma expectations becomes visible.

programmes.name: The Diploma Programme that follows
programmes.description: Six subjects at Higher and Standard Level plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and creativity, activity, service. Assessment shifts decisively towards terminal examinations with a single internally assessed component per subject, which rewards a different set of habits from the MYP's continuous criterion assessment.
programmes.countryNote: The MYP to DP step is where this belt sees the most trouble, and it is specific rather than general: timed examination technique, algebraic fluency without a calculator, and writing to a mark scheme rather than to a criterion descriptor. All three are teachable over a summer and none of them is about intelligence.

programmes.name: IGCSE, for families comparing the two
programmes.description: The alternative route to sixteen, used by most schools near Karama. Terminal written examinations, numerical marks, tiered entry and published past papers. It rewards recall under time pressure and mark-scheme literacy, where the MYP rewards investigation, communication and reflection.
programmes.countryNote: Families in this belt sometimes consider moving a child from an MYP school into an IGCSE school at Year 10. It is doable, and the usual gap runs the other way from the DP transition: the MYP student has strong investigation skills and little experience of timed papers with a fixed mark scheme.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-karama.subjectsIntro: The MYP spans eight subject groups, and the criteria differ between them. These are the groups our MYP specialists cover, with what each set of criteria actually rewards.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Levels are lost most often on investigating patterns, where a student computes cases correctly but never states or justifies a general rule.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. Processing and evaluating is where data handling, uncertainty and limitations are rewarded, and it is the direct ancestor of the Diploma investigation.

subjects.name: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Analysing, organising, producing text, and using language. Students lose levels on analysing by summarising the text rather than interpreting how it achieves its effect, and on organising by writing fluently without a structure a reader can follow.

subjects.name: Language Acquisition
subjects.description: Comprehending spoken and visual text, comprehending written and visual text, communicating, and using language. Phase level rather than year group sets the demand, which parents often misread as their child being placed below their age.

subjects.name: Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, investigating, communicating, and thinking critically. Thinking critically is the discriminator: the levels go to students who evaluate sources and weigh interpretations rather than reporting them.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: Inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution, and evaluating. Design is frequently the subject where a strong student scores lowest, because the marks are in the documented process rather than in the finished product.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively, and responding. The process journal carries a great deal of the assessment, and students who make good work without documenting their thinking lose levels for it.

subjects.name: Physical and Health Education
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, planning for performance, applying and performing, and reflecting and improving performance. Written and reflective components matter as much as physical performance, which surprises both students and parents.

subjects.name: Interdisciplinary units
subjects.description: Assessed on their own criteria: evaluating, synthesising and reflecting across two or more subject groups. These units are frequently the lowest scores on an MYP report because students treat them as a project rather than as an assessed task with descriptors.

subjects.name: Personal Project
subjects.description: Marked on planning, applying skills and reflecting, through a process journal and a report. The quality of the finished product is not what is assessed, which is the fact most families discover too late to act on.

sections.heading: Eight subject groups, four criteria each, and what each criterion rewards
paragraphs: The MYP spans eight subject groups: language and literature, language acquisition, individuals and societies, sciences, mathematics, arts, physical and health education, and design. Every one of them is assessed against four criteria, labelled A to D, each scored from zero to eight against published descriptors. The labels mean different things in different subjects, which is a persistent source of confusion at home: criterion C in mathematics is communicating, while criterion C in sciences is processing and evaluating.

The important point is that only one of the four criteria in most subjects is primarily about knowing things. The other three assess process: how an investigation was designed, how data was handled, how clearly mathematics was communicated, how critically a source was weighed. A student arriving from a content-driven system is often excellent at the first criterion and untrained in the other three, which produces a report that looks like underachievement and is actually unfamiliarity.

This is why buying more content teaching is so often the wrong response to a disappointing MYP report. The question to ask is which criterion the low levels sit in. If a student is scoring seven on knowing and understanding and four on investigating patterns, more mathematics content will change nothing; what is needed is practice at generalising a rule and justifying it, which is a specific and teachable skill with its own descriptors.

Interdisciplinary units deserve a separate mention because they are frequently the lowest scores on an MYP report. They combine two or more subject groups and are assessed on their own criteria around evaluating, synthesising and reflecting. Students treat them as a project rather than as an assessed task, do not read the descriptors, and lose levels they would comfortably have earned. Reading the criteria for an interdisciplinary unit before starting it is close to free marks.

sections.heading: How four criterion levels become a grade from one to seven
paragraphs: The conversion is the part that confuses families most, and understanding it changes how a parent reads a report. Each of the four criteria is scored out of eight, giving a maximum total of thirty-two for a subject. That total is then converted to a final grade from one to seven using grade boundaries published by the IB, applied by the school. The boundaries are bands rather than percentages, so a total sitting at the top of one band and a total at the bottom of the next look very similar on paper and produce different grades.

Two consequences follow. The first is that a single weak criterion can cost a whole grade, because the four scores are added. A student with sevens in three criteria and a three in the fourth totals twenty-four; a student with sixes across all four totals twenty-four as well. They look like very different students in class and receive the same grade, and the first of those two has a much clearer route to improvement because the problem is localised.

The second is that the cheapest grade improvement available in the MYP is usually the weakest criterion, not the strongest subject. Lifting a three to a five in one criterion is worth as much as lifting every other criterion by half a level, and it is far more achievable because the descriptors for that one criterion can be read, practised against and marked. This is the arithmetic that should drive a tutoring decision, and it is almost never explained to parents.

Reports also carry a complication worth knowing: not every criterion is assessed in every reporting period. A school assesses criteria across a cycle of tasks, so a report may show levels for two criteria and nothing for the others, or carry a level from a task several weeks old. Ask the subject teacher which criteria were assessed in which tasks, and ask for the task-specific clarifications that accompanied them. That request is routine and it transforms what a parent can see.

sections.heading: The task-specific clarification: the document that tells you the answer
paragraphs: Every assessed MYP task should come with a task-specific clarification, in which the teacher rewrites the generic criterion descriptors in the language of that particular task. It states, in advance, what a student has to do to reach the top band. It is handed out with the task. A large share of the MYP students we meet in this belt have either never read one or have read it after submitting the work.

The reason this matters so much is that MYP descriptors are written in general terms and are genuinely hard to apply without translation. A generic descriptor asking a student to select and apply mathematical problem-solving techniques to discover complex patterns is not actionable on its own. The task-specific version tells the student that, for this task, they need to find the rule for the nth term, justify it, and test it on a case outside the given data. That is actionable.

The habit we teach first, in almost every MYP subject, is to read the clarification before planning the work and then to write the plan against it line by line. Every phrase in the top band becomes a thing to do. Students who adopt this stop losing levels to omission, which is the single biggest source of lost levels in the programme: the work is good, and one requirement in the descriptor was simply never addressed.

The second habit is to self-assess against the clarification before submitting. The student reads each descriptor phrase and points to where in their work it is satisfied. Where they cannot point, they fix it. This takes fifteen minutes, it is entirely the student's own work, and it reliably moves levels. A tutor who teaches that habit well makes themselves progressively less necessary, which is the correct direction of travel for MYP tutoring.

sections.heading: The Personal Project: marked on process, not on the product
paragraphs: The Personal Project runs in MYP 5 and is the component families in this belt ask about most. A student chooses a goal, works towards it over an extended period, keeps a process journal, and submits a report. It is assessed against its own small set of criteria covering planning, applying skills and reflecting. The crucial fact, and the one most often learned too late, is that the quality of the finished object is not what is being assessed.

Students therefore pour their effort into the wrong place. A beautifully made product with a thin process journal scores poorly; a modest product with rigorous planning, evidenced skill development and genuine critical reflection scores well. Explaining this early changes how a student spends six months. Explaining it in the final fortnight changes very little, because the journal evidence cannot be retrofitted honestly and should not be.

The process journal is the engine of the whole component. It is assessed evidence rather than a diary, which means it needs dated entries showing decisions, dead ends, sources consulted, skills attempted and failures analysed. A journal that records only what went well is useless to the criteria, because the criteria reward evaluating a process rather than reporting a success. Teaching a student what to record, and how often, is perhaps two sessions of work with a disproportionate effect.

The boundary is absolute. An IB Gram tutor will interrogate the goal, help narrow it until it is specific enough to be evidenced, teach the skills the student has chosen to develop, explain what each criterion requires and give feedback on the student's own journal and report. An IB Gram tutor will not supply the goal, produce the product, write the report, rewrite the student's prose or create journal entries. The school's supervisor remains the supervisor and the academic-honesty declaration remains your child's.

sections.heading: MYP 5 into the Diploma: the three gaps that actually cause trouble
paragraphs: This is the transition where this belt sees the most difficulty, and it is specific rather than general. An MYP student arriving in DP1 usually has better investigation skills, better reflective writing and better independent research habits than a student arriving from IGCSE. What they often lack is three things, and all three are teachable in a summer.

The first is timed examination technique. MYP assessment is continuous and criterion-based, and a student can reach MYP 5 having sat very few examinations under strict timing. The Diploma is decided largely by terminal papers. Question triage, time allocation by marks available, writing a partial answer rather than nothing, and finishing a paper are all skills rather than knowledge, and a student who has never practised them loses marks across every subject at once.

The second is algebraic fluency without a calculator, which matters for anyone taking mathematics or a science. MYP mathematics rewards process and explanation and permits a calculator for most tasks. DP mathematics Paper 1 is sat without one, and Diploma physics and chemistry assume rearrangement as a routine step. A student who is strong at investigating patterns can be slow at manipulating an expression, and that slowness costs marks in three subjects.

The third is writing to a mark scheme rather than to a criterion descriptor. A descriptor describes a quality; a mark scheme lists awardable points. The habits differ: in the MYP a student writes a coherent piece addressing a quality, while in the Diploma a student writes an answer shaped to the command term with each creditable point made explicitly. Students who do not make the switch write good prose and collect partial marks. Two or three sessions on real past papers with the scheme visible is usually enough to establish the difference.

sections.heading: eAssessment or school-assessed: ask which route your school uses
paragraphs: MYP 5 can end in two quite different ways depending on the school. Some schools enter students for MYP eAssessment, which uses on-screen examinations and ePortfolios and leads to the IB MYP Certificate. Others assess internally across the five years and award school-based grades without external examinations. Both are legitimate and both are in use in Dubai. They demand completely different final-year preparation.

Where eAssessment applies, the final year contains externally assessed on-screen examinations, which reintroduces exactly the timed, unseen-paper demand the rest of the MYP does not emphasise. Preparation therefore looks much more like IGCSE revision than like criterion work, and a student who has spent five years on continuous assessment needs explicit practice at sitting a paper. Where it does not apply, the final year is a continuation of criterion-based tasks and the Personal Project, and preparation should look nothing like examination revision.

The practical instruction for a Karama family is to ask the school directly, in MYP 4 rather than in the last term of MYP 5, which route it uses and which subjects it enters for eAssessment where the route is mixed. Schools do sometimes enter students for some subjects and not others. The answer determines whether the final year needs examination technique or criterion depth, and buying the wrong one is a wasted year of tutoring.

Either way, the conversation about Diploma readiness should happen at the same time. A school-assessed MYP 5 means a student may arrive in DP1 with very little examination experience, which makes the summer bridge more important rather than less. An eAssessment route gives a student some of that experience already, which changes the bridge from technique-building to consolidation. Tutoring planned without knowing which case applies is tutoring planned blind.

sections.heading: What MYP tutoring costs in Dubai, and why the brief matters more than the rate
paragraphs: Published Dubai rates divide by tier rather than by programme. Budget online tutoring is advertised from roughly AED 45 to AED 150 an hour, with EdFlik publishing AED 45 to AED 65 and Tutopiya quoting from AED 33 to AED 52. Qualified subject tutors working online are quoted at AED 150 to AED 300, with Unitors publishing IGCSE tuition from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. IB specialists are quoted at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, TutorChase listing AED 270 and Bestimate's 2026 Dubai rate table giving AED 200 to AED 450 and upwards. Premium named tutors reach AED 650 at BartyED.

For the MYP specifically, the rate band is less predictive of value than the brief you give the tutor. A tutor at the top of the mid-band who has never read an MYP task-specific clarification will teach good content and leave the weak criterion untouched. A tutor lower in the band who asks for the clarification, the task and the criterion levels before the first session is doing the thing that moves the grade. This is a question you can ask on the phone, and it separates MYP-literate tutors from subject tutors very quickly.

Monthly, Bestimate's estimates for a weekly one-hour session run AED 240 to AED 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to AED 1,200 mid-band and AED 1,000 to AED 2,000 and above for specialist examination-year work. Packages circulating in this market include around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to AED 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions, the latter being higher because travel sits inside the hour. Bestimate puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to AED 350, with independent home tutors advertising AED 200 to AED 500.

MYP tutoring also tends to need fewer total hours than Diploma tutoring if it is briefed correctly, because much of the gain comes from habits rather than from content. Teaching a student to read a clarification, plan against it and self-assess before submitting is a handful of sessions with an effect that persists across every subject. That is a genuinely cheap intervention, and it is the one we would start with for most families here. For IB Gram's own arrangements, begin with the free trial lesson and the consultation.

sections.heading: Why MYP help travels badly to a flat and well over video
paragraphs: MYP tutoring is unusually document-heavy. A session works from the task, the generic criteria, the school's task-specific clarification, the student's draft and the process journal, often all at once. Four documents and a draft are easier to hold side by side on a screen with annotation than on a dining table in a Karama apartment, and the annotated version is retained for the next session rather than lost in a margin.

The pool argument is stronger here than in most subjects, because MYP literacy is rarer than subject knowledge. Plenty of tutors can teach Year 9 mathematics. Far fewer can look at a criterion B level of four and say what specifically is missing from a generalisation. A Karama family hiring someone who can attend in person is choosing from tutors living nearby and free at the student's hour, and the chance that one of them is MYP-literate in the right subject group is low. Online changes the constraint from postcode to diary.

The practical detail favours online too. MYP students in this belt generally travel further to school than their IGCSE neighbours, because the nearest IB continuum schools sit outside the Karama grid in Al Garhoud, Deira or Al Barsha. A longer commute means a later arrival home, which makes a session that needs no travel on the tutor's side considerably easier to schedule. The in-home band is also higher at AED 180 to AED 500 than the AED 150 to AED 300 online band, and that difference buys a drive.

The honest exception is a younger MYP 1 or MYP 2 student who will not focus over video, where a person in the room genuinely helps. For MYP 4 and 5 students working on a Personal Project or a criterion weakness it rarely decides anything. IB Gram does not offer in-home visits anywhere in the UAE — home tutoring is a service we provide only in India — so where a child needs someone physically present we will say so rather than sell an online session as a substitute.

sections.heading: Regulators, permits and the limits on what a tutor may do
paragraphs: Dubai's private schools are regulated by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which on the UAE government's own description is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. In 2024-25 the sector held 387,441 students across 227 private schools offering seventeen curricula, with the International Baccalaureate accounting for 7 per cent of enrolment, UK curriculum 37 per cent, Indian 26 and US 14. Dubai's 2026-27 intake adds seven new private schools, four UK curriculum and three International Baccalaureate, creating 16,846 new places, after six opened during 2025-26 and enrolment rose 6 per cent.

KHDA also requires Arabic, Islamic Education and social or moral studies in every Dubai private school regardless of its licensed curriculum, with separate classes organised for Arab and non-Arab students, instructional time calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit, and no different or additional content permitted for those subjects without prior Ministry of Education approval. MYP students carry those subjects alongside the eight subject groups, which is why an MYP week is fuller than the programme model alone suggests.

Private tutoring is lawful and regulated by permit. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and is open to teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged fifteen to eighteen, and university students, applied for through MoHRE's own private tutor licensing service. Tutoring without a permit carries fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and no fine schedule has been published, so any specific figure quoted to you is unverified.

None of this makes anyone official. IB Gram is not approved, accredited or licensed by KHDA, the Ministry of Education, MoHRE or the IB, and a KHDA Educational Services Permit is a specific authorisation for training institutes with premises in Dubai that we neither hold nor claim. On academic honesty the line does not move: we teach, question, explain criteria and give feedback on the student's own work. We will not produce a Personal Project, write a report, create journal entries or complete any assessed task, and we will not supply IB subject guides or assessment materials as downloads.

faqs.question: What do the letters and numbers on an MYP report actually mean?
faqs.answer: Each subject is assessed against four criteria labelled A to D, and each criterion is scored from zero to eight against published descriptors. The four scores are added, giving a maximum of thirty-two, and that total converts to a final grade from one to seven using published grade boundaries applied by the school. The labels mean different things in different subjects: criterion C is communicating in mathematics and processing and evaluating in sciences. Ask the subject teacher which criteria were assessed in which tasks, because not every criterion appears in every reporting cycle.

faqs.question: My child knows the content but scores a four. Why?
faqs.answer: Because only one of the four criteria in most subjects is primarily about knowing things. The others assess process: how an investigation was designed, how data was handled, how clearly the work communicates, how critically a source was weighed. A student arriving from a content-driven system is often excellent at criterion A and untrained in the rest, which looks like underachievement and is unfamiliarity. More content teaching will not change it; practice against the specific weak criterion's descriptors will, and that is a different purchase entirely.

faqs.question: What is a task-specific clarification and should we have seen one?
faqs.answer: It is the document in which the teacher rewrites the generic criterion descriptors in the language of a particular task, stating in advance what a top-band response contains. It should be handed out with the assessed task. Many students in this belt have never read one, or read it after submitting. Asking the school for it is routine and it transforms what a parent can see, because the exact requirements stop being abstract. The habit worth building is planning the work against each phrase in the top band.

faqs.question: How do we decide which subject to get MYP tutoring in first?
faqs.answer: Look for the lowest single criterion level rather than the lowest subject grade. Because the four criteria are added, a student with sevens in three criteria and a three in the fourth gets the same total as a student with sixes throughout, but the first has a localised and fixable problem. Lifting one criterion from a three to a five is worth as much as raising every other criterion by half a level and is far more achievable, because one set of descriptors can be read, practised against and marked.

faqs.question: Why is my child losing levels on investigating patterns in MYP maths?
faqs.answer: Almost always because the general rule is missing or unjustified. The criterion rewards selecting and applying problem-solving techniques to find a pattern, describing it as a general rule, and then justifying or verifying it, often on a case outside the given data. Students compute every example correctly, present a neat table and stop, which answers a different question. Teaching the sequence — find the pattern, state the rule algebraically, justify it, test it beyond the data — usually moves this criterion in a handful of sessions.

faqs.question: Is the Personal Project marked on how good the finished product is?
faqs.answer: No, and this is the fact most families learn too late. It is assessed on planning, applying skills and reflecting, evidenced through a process journal and a report. A beautifully made product with a thin journal scores poorly; a modest product with rigorous planning, documented skill development and genuine critical reflection scores well. The journal needs dated entries showing decisions, dead ends, sources and failures analysed, not a record of what went well. Knowing this in the first month changes how a student spends six months.

faqs.question: How much can a tutor help with the Personal Project?
faqs.answer: Within firm limits. A tutor can interrogate the goal, help narrow it until it is specific enough to be evidenced, teach the skills the student has chosen to develop, explain what each criterion requires and give feedback on the student's own journal and report. A tutor cannot supply the goal, produce the product, write the report, rewrite the student's prose or create journal entries. The school's supervisor remains the supervisor and the academic-honesty declaration remains your child's. Any service offering to produce a project is offering a malpractice risk.

faqs.question: Why are interdisciplinary unit scores often the lowest on the report?
faqs.answer: Because students treat them as projects rather than as assessed tasks with their own criteria. Interdisciplinary units combine two or more subject groups and are assessed on criteria around evaluating, synthesising and reflecting across them. Students who never read those descriptors lose levels they would comfortably have earned on work they did well. Reading the criteria before starting, and planning the piece so that each descriptor phrase is visibly addressed, is close to free marks and takes one session to teach properly.

faqs.question: What actually goes wrong when MYP students start the Diploma?
faqs.answer: Three things, all teachable. Timed examination technique, because MYP assessment is continuous and a student may have sat very few strictly timed papers. Algebraic fluency without a calculator, which matters for mathematics, physics and chemistry, since DP maths Paper 1 permits none. And writing to a mark scheme rather than to a criterion descriptor, because a descriptor describes a quality while a scheme lists awardable points. MYP students usually arrive with better research and reflective habits than their IGCSE peers; these three gaps are the counterweight.

faqs.question: Should we do a summer bridge between MYP 5 and DP1?
faqs.answer: For most students heading into mathematics or a science, yes, and it should be planned from the chosen DP option block rather than from the MYP report. Short daily calculator-free algebra sets, a few sessions of mark-scheme literacy on real past papers, and some timed practice are enough to remove most of the friction from the first term. It is a cheap intervention compared with catching up in DP1, and it is more effective than a general pre-Diploma course covering content the student will be taught anyway.

faqs.question: Does our MYP school use eAssessment or internal assessment?
faqs.answer: Ask the school directly, and ask in MYP 4 rather than in the final term of MYP 5. Some schools enter students for MYP eAssessment, which uses on-screen examinations and ePortfolios and leads to the MYP Certificate; others assess internally across the five years and award school-based grades. Schools sometimes enter students for some subjects and not others. The answer decides whether the final year needs examination technique or criterion depth, and preparing for the wrong one wastes a year of tutoring.

faqs.question: What does MYP tutoring cost in Dubai?
faqs.answer: Published rates divide by tier rather than by programme. Budget online tutoring is advertised from roughly AED 45 to AED 150 an hour, with EdFlik at AED 45 to AED 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to AED 52. Qualified subject tutors online are quoted at AED 150 to AED 300, with Unitors publishing IB from AED 200, and IB specialists at AED 200 to AED 450 and above, TutorChase listing AED 270. For the MYP, the brief matters more than the band: insist the tutor works from the task, the criteria and the school's clarification.

faqs.question: Do MYP students in Karama have to travel for school, and does that affect scheduling?
faqs.answer: Usually, yes. The schools immediately around Karama and Oud Metha run IGCSE rather than the MYP, so MYP families here generally commute out to Al Garhoud, Deira or Al Barsha. That makes the day longer than for their IGCSE neighbours and pushes sessions later. Online delivery helps precisely because it removes the tutor's travel from the equation as well, so a session can start as soon as the student is home rather than after a second journey. Weekend slots carry more of the plan for families further out.

faqs.question: Does the MYP leave room for the UAE mandatory subjects?
faqs.answer: It has to, and it is one reason an MYP week feels fuller than the programme model suggests. KHDA requires Arabic, Islamic Education and social or moral studies in every Dubai private school regardless of the licensed curriculum, with separate classes organised for Arab and non-Arab students and instructional time calculated on a forty-minute lesson unit. No different or additional content is permitted for those subjects without prior Ministry of Education approval. For tutoring planning this is simply timetable arithmetic: the free hours in the week are fewer than eight subject groups imply.

faqs.question: Will a tutor make my child dependent on tutoring?
faqs.answer: Done properly, the opposite. The core MYP habits — read the task-specific clarification, plan against each phrase in the top band, self-assess by pointing to where each requirement is met before submitting — are skills the student performs alone. A tutor who teaches those well becomes progressively less necessary, which is the correct direction of travel. We would rather run six weeks that change a habit than two years that supply answers, and if the levels stop needing us we will say so rather than extend a plan.

intro.heading: A year with no examination to count down to, and three dates that matter instead
paragraphs: The Middle Years Programme is the hardest IB programme for a parent to read, and the reason is structural rather than linguistic. There is no terminal public examination in MYP 1 to MYP 4, no syllabus content list of the kind an IGCSE parent can look up, and no single grade that behaves like a percentage. Instead there are four criteria per subject, each scored from zero to eight, converted to a one-to-seven grade by boundaries the school publishes. A report arrives, the numbers move in different directions, and nobody can tell whether anything is wrong.

That is usually what brings a family in this catchment to search for an IB MYP tutor in Dubai Knowledge Park. The honest first answer is not a tutor at all - it is a reading of the report. A student scoring 7 on criterion A in sciences and 3 on criterion C has a data-processing problem, not a science problem, and buying general science tutoring would spend money in the wrong place. The criteria are diagnostic if you know what each one measures, and almost nobody is shown.

Three dates do anchor the Middle Years year, and they are the ones worth planning around. The first is each reporting cycle, because that is when criterion scores are published and comparable against the last set. The second is the school's internal deadline for the Personal Project in MYP 5, which arrives earlier in the year than families expect and is marked out of twenty-four across three criteria. The third is the transition into the Diploma or into IGCSE, where subject choices made in MYP 4 and MYP 5 begin to bite.

Where a school enters candidates for MYP eAssessment - on-screen examinations and ePortfolios leading to the IB MYP Certificate - there is a fourth anchor, and it sits in the May session. Not every school in this belt does this, and whether yours does is a question for the MYP coordinator rather than an assumption. Where it applies, the preparation is genuinely different from ordinary unit work, because the on-screen examinations ask students to apply criteria to unseen material under time pressure.

Knowledge Park itself is an education free zone off Al Sufouh Road, holding university campuses and training institutes rather than homes, so families running this search live in Al Sufouh, Media City, Barsha Heights, The Greens or the Marina towers. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai; a tutor attending a UAE address is a service we run only in India. Lessons here are one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, which for the Middle Years Programme matters in a particular way: the tutor has to work from the school's own unit plans and task sheets, and sharing those on a screen is easier than carrying them to a kitchen table.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme, years four and five
programmes.description: Where consequences begin. Subject choices narrow, extended and standard mathematics separate, and the Personal Project runs through MYP 5 alongside everything else. Criterion scores in these two years are what a Diploma coordinator looks at when advising on Higher Level choices, which makes them the first scores in a student's record with real downstream weight.
programmes.countryNote: In this belt, MYP 4 is when the extended against standard mathematics decision is made, and it is the single most consequential choice in the programme. Extended mathematics is the realistic preparation for Diploma Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level; standard mathematics is not, and the gap usually becomes visible in the first term of Year 12 rather than at the moment of choosing.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme, after MYP 5
programmes.description: Six subjects at Higher or Standard Level plus the Extended Essay, Theory of Knowledge and CAS. The structural shift is from criterion-referenced reporting to published assessment weightings and external papers, and students who have only ever been assessed against criteria find the first set of examination-style marks disorienting. The skills transfer; the framing does not.
programmes.countryNote: Dubai's 2026-27 intake adds seven new private schools - four UK curriculum and three International Baccalaureate - creating 16,846 new places, after six opened during 2025-26 and enrolment rose 6 per cent. For an MYP 4 family in this belt that widens the post-16 field, which makes the subject-choice conversation worth having a year earlier than it usually happens.

programmes.name: IGCSE, the other route out of MYP
programmes.description: Some students in this belt move from the Middle Years Programme into IGCSE at fourteen, usually because of a school change. The shift is from criterion-referenced tasks to terminal written papers on a published content list, with Core and Extended tiering, and it suits students who prefer a defined body of content to an open-ended investigation.
programmes.countryNote: A move from MYP 3 into Year 10 IGCSE in this belt requires an honest look at content coverage, because the Middle Years Programme does not march through a syllabus in the same order. Mathematics is usually the subject needing bridging work, and a term of targeted support before the move is far cheaper than catching up during Year 10.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-knowledge-park.subjectsIntro: These are the Middle Years subject groups Knowledge Park families most often ask about, with the criterion that usually explains a disappointing report named.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Four criteria: knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Investigating patterns is where strong arithmetic students lose marks, because it asks for generalisation and justification rather than correct answers.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: Criteria cover knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. Processing and evaluating is the reliable weak point and the one that predicts Diploma science difficulty most accurately.

subjects.name: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Analysing, organising, producing text, and using language. Students who read widely still lose marks under organising, because an essay that is insightful but unstructured sits in a lower band than one that is competent and clearly built.

subjects.name: Language Acquisition
subjects.description: Assessed by phase rather than by year group, which is why two students in the same class can be working towards different descriptors. Listening and speaking criteria are the ones families most often discover are dragging the grade down.

subjects.name: Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, investigating, communicating, and thinking critically. Thinking critically is where the marks are, and it requires evaluating sources and perspectives rather than describing events accurately.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: Inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution, and evaluating. The design cycle is marked on process rather than on the finished product, which surprises students who produce something impressive with no documented development.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively, and responding. The process journal carries more weight than students expect, and a strong performer with a thin journal loses marks across two criteria.

subjects.name: Physical and Health Education
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, planning for performance, applying and performing, and reflecting and improving performance. The written criteria mean a highly capable athlete can score poorly, which is a frequent source of confusion on reports.

subjects.name: The Personal Project
subjects.description: Marked out of 24 across three criteria: planning, applying skills, and reflecting. The process journal is the evidence base for all three, and projects fail on documentation rather than on ambition.

subjects.name: Arabic as a First or Additional Language
subjects.description: Arabic is mandatory in all Dubai private schools whatever the licensed curriculum, and KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students because expectations and the language of instruction differ. Support must match the pathway the school has placed the student in.

sections.heading: Reading the report: what each criterion is actually measuring
paragraphs: A Middle Years report is a set of diagnostic instruments that most families treat as a verdict. Each subject carries four criteria, each scored from zero to eight, and the school converts the total out of thirty-two into a one-to-seven grade using published boundaries. Ask for those boundaries - they are not the same across subjects, and a total of twenty-two can convert differently in sciences and in language and literature.

The pattern across the four criteria is where the information is. In sciences, a high score on knowing and understanding with a low one on processing and evaluating means the student holds the content and cannot handle data - uncertainties, graphs, drawing a conclusion the evidence supports. That is a narrow, fixable gap and it is the single best predictor of difficulty in Diploma sciences two years later. General science tutoring would spend a term in the wrong place.

In mathematics, a high knowing and understanding with a low investigating patterns means a student who computes accurately and cannot generalise or justify. That is the criterion Diploma mathematics leans on hardest, and it responds to a specific kind of work - being asked to find a rule, test it, and explain why it holds - rather than to more exercises. In language and literature, a strong analysing score with a weak organising score describes a student with insight and no structure, which is two or three sessions of work rather than a term.

The table below sets out what each subject group's criteria measure and what a low score in each one actually indicates. It is written to be read with a report in hand. The useful outcome of ten minutes with it is usually a decision not to buy general subject tutoring, which is why no competitor page in this market publishes anything like it.

sections.heading: The Personal Project counted backwards from the school deadline
paragraphs: The Personal Project is the one Middle Years component with a hard deadline and a published mark scheme, and it is where the calendar matters most. It is marked out of twenty-four across three criteria - planning, applying skills, and reflecting, at eight marks each - and the process journal is the evidence base for all three. Projects fail on documentation rather than on ambition, which is why the timeline is the thing to get right rather than the idea.

Count backwards from the school's internal deadline, which sits well ahead of any IB submission window and is the date that governs your child's term. Working back: the report is written in the final weeks; the product or outcome is completed before that; the bulk of the applying-skills work sits in the middle terms; and the goal, criteria and planning are set at the start. The reflection criterion is the one students treat as a final task, and it is the one that most needs to run throughout.

The commonest failure in this catchment is a strong student with an ambitious goal and an empty process journal. They have done real work and cannot evidence it, because the journal was never a weekly habit. The marks for planning and reflecting both depend on documentation written as the work happened, and reconstructing it afterwards reads exactly like reconstruction. Fifteen minutes a week from the start is worth more than any amount of effort in the final month.

A tutor's role here is coaching rather than production. We can help a student test whether a goal is achievable with the time and resources available, explain what each criterion rewards, ask the questions that generate genuine reflection, and comment on a draft the student has written. We do not choose the goal, make the product, or write the report. The school authenticates that the work is the student's own, and the consequence of a false authentication falls on the student.

sections.heading: What eight weeks of Middle Years support can realistically achieve
paragraphs: Eight weeks between reporting cycles is the block families in this catchment most often ask for, and it is a sensible length for the Middle Years Programme precisely because the school provides the measurement at each end. The honest answer about what it can do depends almost entirely on whether a criterion was named at the start.

A block aimed at one criterion works. Eight weeks on processing and evaluating in sciences - uncertainties, graph construction, drawing conclusions the data supports, evaluating a method - produces a measurable change in that criterion score, because the skill is narrow and the descriptors are explicit about what each band requires. Eight weeks on investigating patterns in mathematics does the same. Eight weeks of general subject tutoring produces a vague improvement that nobody can locate in the next report.

What eight weeks cannot do is change a student's whole relationship with school. A twelve-year-old who is disorganised across every subject has an approaches-to-learning problem rather than a subject problem, and the intervention is about systems - how work is recorded, how a task sheet is read, how a deadline is planned backwards. That is genuinely teachable and it takes longer than eight weeks, but it also pays across all eight subject groups rather than one.

The practical shape that works is a single criterion, in a single subject, with the school's own task sheets as the material and the next report as the measure. Where more is wrong than that, sequence it. A Middle Years student doing three subjects of tutoring a week has no time left for the independent work that criterion scores actually reward, and the usual result is that nothing moves.

sections.heading: The MYP 4 mathematics decision and why it outranks everything else
paragraphs: In MYP 4 most schools in this belt separate mathematics into standard and extended, and that choice is the most consequential thing in the whole programme. Extended mathematics is the realistic preparation for Diploma Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level. Standard mathematics is not, and the gap does not announce itself at the point of choosing - it appears in the first term of Year 12, by which point the Diploma course is already running.

The decision is usually made on criterion A, knowing and understanding, because that is the score that looks like a maths grade. It should be made on criterion B, investigating patterns, because that is the criterion measuring the skill extended mathematics and Diploma mathematics both lean on - generalising a rule, testing it, justifying why it holds. A student strong on A and weak on B will find extended mathematics harder than their report predicts, and that is exactly the student a term of targeted work can rescue.

The reverse pattern matters too. A student with a solid B and a middling A is often placed in standard mathematics on the strength of the A score, and is capable of extended with support on the computational fluency. That case is worth arguing, and it is worth arguing with evidence - a timed extended-level task, marked against the descriptors - rather than with parental conviction, because schools respond to the first and not the second.

Where the decision has already gone the wrong way, the honest options are to make the case for a change while timetabling still allows it, or to plan the Diploma around Applications and Interpretation, which is a different course rather than an easier one and is accepted by a substantial range of university courses. What should not happen is finding out in Year 12. Ask in MYP 4 which mathematics route is intended and on which criterion the recommendation rests.
bullets: Extended mathematics in MYP 4-5 is the realistic preparation for Higher Level Analysis and Approaches
The decision should rest on criterion B, investigating patterns, not criterion A
A strong A with a weak B predicts difficulty that the overall grade hides

sections.heading: eAssessment, where it applies, and how it differs from unit work
paragraphs: Some schools enter MYP 5 candidates for IB MYP eAssessment - on-screen examinations and ePortfolios leading to the IB MYP Certificate - and others do not. Which applies at your child's school is a question for the MYP coordinator, and it changes the final year materially. Where a school does not enter candidates, MYP 5 is assessed internally against criteria throughout, and the Personal Project is the only component with a hard external-style deadline.

Where eAssessment does apply, the preparation is different from ordinary unit work in a way worth understanding. The on-screen examinations present unseen material and ask students to apply criteria to it under time pressure, which rewards students who understand what a criterion is asking rather than those who have learned a unit's content. Students who have treated criteria descriptors as administrative language rather than as instructions find this genuinely difficult.

The ePortfolio components are closer to ordinary coursework but still carry the same honesty boundary: the work must be the student's own, and the school authenticates it. Preparation for these is about process and documentation, which is the same skill the Personal Project rewards, so a student who has built good journal habits is already most of the way there.

We do not publish IB session or results dates on these pages. ibo.org blocks automated access and no date in this project has been confirmed from the IB itself, so the exact eAssessment session dates, deadlines and release dates come from the school's MYP coordinator. What can be said is that the session UAE schools work towards sits in May, and that the school's internal deadlines - which are the ones that govern your child's term - sit well ahead of it.
bullets: Not every school enters MYP 5 candidates for eAssessment - ask the MYP coordinator
On-screen examinations apply criteria to unseen material under time pressure

sections.heading: Where Middle Years tutoring money gets wasted in this catchment
paragraphs: Middle Years spending goes wrong in predictable ways, and naming them is more useful than quoting rates. The first waste is buying a subject when the report named a criterion. A family sees a 4 in sciences, buys weekly science tutoring, and a term later the criterion that was low is still low because nobody worked on data processing specifically. The report told them what to buy and the subject name got in the way.

The second waste is starting too early with too much. A Middle Years student in MYP 1 or MYP 2 with three weekly tutoring sessions has no unstructured time and no reason to develop independent study habits, and the criteria reward exactly those habits. For younger students the highest-value support is usually a short block on approaches to learning - how to read a task sheet, how to plan backwards from a deadline, how to keep a usable record - rather than subject content.

The third waste is the Personal Project rescue. A project with an empty process journal four weeks before the deadline cannot be fixed by money, because the marks for planning and reflecting depend on documentation written as the work happened. Fifteen minutes a week from the start costs nothing and is worth more than any late intervention. Any provider offering to produce the project is offering something that puts the student at risk rather than helping them.

On rates, published figures in this market run from roughly AED 33 to 65 an hour at the budget end, which generally means a university student, through AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor online, with specialist work quoted at AED 200 to 450 and above. In-home one-to-one is quoted at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel inside the price, and monthly packages run around AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour visits against roughly AED 799 for eight online sessions. Those are other providers' published figures. IB Gram publishes no rate card here; the trial lesson and the consultation are free.

sections.heading: Honesty on the Personal Project, and on who may teach
paragraphs: The Personal Project is where academic honesty is tested in this programme, because it is a long independent piece produced under a deadline by a fifteen-year-old. The boundary is clear. A tutor may help a student test whether a goal is achievable, explain what the three criteria reward, model how a process journal entry is written, ask the questions that produce genuine reflection, and comment on a draft the student has written.

A tutor may not choose the goal, make the product, or write the report. The school authenticates that the work is the student's own, and if that authentication is untrue the consequence falls on the student rather than on whoever helped. One site ranking in this market sells completed internal assessments at a published price; that transaction transfers the entire risk onto a teenager, which is worth saying plainly whenever a provider offers it.

Materials follow the same logic. We reference the IB subject guides and the Personal Project guide, cite them and point to the official source. We do not reproduce them or distribute them as downloads, because they are the board's copyright. Where a school's own unit plans and task sheets are the working material, those come from the student and stay with the student rather than being circulated.

There is a question about who may teach, too. Abu Dhabi's ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from giving paid private tuition to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE private tuition permit carries a code of conduct barring the same arrangement. Those are press-reported positions and should be verified against the current policy document, but the principle travels: engaging your child's own classroom teacher privately is the arrangement most likely to put that teacher in breach. The permit itself is checkable - it was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years through MoHRE, and tutoring without one carries fines and penalties under the applicable laws, with no fine schedule published.

sections.heading: KHDA, the mandatory subjects and the Middle Years timetable
paragraphs: Private education in Dubai is overseen by KHDA, the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. The sector ran 227 private schools and 387,441 students in 2024-25 across seventeen curricula, with International Baccalaureate programmes accounting for 7 per cent of enrolment. Inspection reports are public and name subject-level strengths, which makes them the most useful comparison available between two schools running the Middle Years Programme.

The mandatory UAE subjects apply to the Middle Years Programme exactly as they do to every other curriculum. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are required in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with KHDA's requirements to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year. Instructional time is calculated against a forty-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the weekly total is met, and at least twenty-five minutes is advised for any mandatory subject lesson.

That matters for a Middle Years timetable more than for most, because the programme already requires all eight subject groups to be taught every year. Fitting eight subject groups plus three mandatory subjects into a week is tight, and the practical consequence families notice is that individual subjects get fewer periods than they would in a narrower curriculum. It is one reason a Middle Years student can feel busy and under-taught in the same term.

KHDA also requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, because curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ, and combined classes for the two groups are prohibited. Schools must ensure teachers of Arabic and Islamic Education hold appropriate KHDA approval, and for the mandatory subjects the use of different or additional content without prior permission from the Ministry of Education is prohibited, which constrains what any tutor can legitimately offer in those subjects.

process.title: Send the report, with the criterion scores
process.description: Not the summary grade - the individual criterion scores for each subject. The pattern across the four criteria is what tells us whether this is a content problem, a data-handling problem or a structure problem, and those need entirely different work.

process.title: Ask the school for the grade boundaries
process.description: The conversion from a total out of thirty-two to a one-to-seven grade differs by subject. Without the boundaries, a parent cannot tell whether a total of twenty-two is a comfortable 5 or a borderline 4, and that changes how urgent anything is.

process.title: Name one criterion for the block
process.description: One criterion, one subject, with the next reporting cycle as the measure. A block with a named target produces a result a parent can see in the school's own report; a block aimed at a subject produces an impression.

process.title: A free trial on a live unit
process.description: The tutor works on whatever task the student has in front of them this week, using the school's own task sheet and criteria descriptors. That shows whether explanations land and whether the tutor can read a descriptor properly.

process.title: Deal with the Personal Project early or not at all
process.description: If the project is live, the useful work is goal feasibility and journal habits in the first weeks. Four weeks before the deadline with an empty journal, we will say honestly that the planning and reflecting marks are largely already determined.

process.title: Review at the school's next report
process.description: The school provides the measurement, which is better than any internal test we could run. If the named criterion has moved, the block worked. If it has not, we change the approach or the tutor rather than extending on hope.

whyPoints.title: The report is the brief
whyPoints.description: We start from the criterion scores rather than the subject name, because the criteria are diagnostic and the subject name is not. That frequently means advising against the tutoring a family came to buy.

whyPoints.title: The school's materials, not ours
whyPoints.description: Middle Years marks are awarded against criteria applied to the school's own unit tasks. A tutor working from a generic scheme is working on a different course from the one the student is being assessed on.

whyPoints.title: One criterion at a time
whyPoints.description: A named criterion in a named subject, measured by the school's next report. It is the only structure in this programme where a parent can tell afterwards whether the money did anything.

whyPoints.title: The MYP 4 maths decision taken seriously
whyPoints.description: Extended against standard mathematics is the most consequential choice in the programme, and it should rest on investigating patterns rather than on knowing and understanding. We will produce the evidence for that conversation.

whyPoints.title: Personal Project coaching, not production
whyPoints.description: Feasibility, criteria, journal habits and feedback on the student's own draft. We do not choose goals, make products or write reports, and we explain why that protects the student.

whyPoints.title: Honest about what tutoring cannot fix
whyPoints.description: An empty process journal four weeks out, or whole-school disorganisation in eight weeks. We say so, because the alternative is selling something that will not work and then explaining why afterwards.

faqs.question: How do I read an MYP report when the numbers all move in different directions?
faqs.answer: Read the criteria rather than the grade. Each subject has four, scored zero to eight, and the pattern is the information. In sciences, a high knowing and understanding with a low processing and evaluating means the content is held and the data handling is not. In mathematics, a high knowing and understanding with a low investigating patterns means accurate computation without generalisation. Ask the school for the published grade boundaries too, because the conversion from thirty-two marks to a one-to-seven grade differs between subjects.

faqs.question: My son has a 7 in criterion A and a 3 in criterion C in sciences. What should we actually buy?
faqs.answer: Not general science tutoring. That pattern says he holds the content and cannot process data - graphs, uncertainties, drawing a conclusion the evidence supports, evaluating a method. It is a narrow and highly fixable gap, and it happens to be the best available predictor of difficulty in Diploma sciences two years later. An eight-week block aimed at that one criterion, using his school's own task sheets, is the right purchase, and the next report is the measure of whether it worked.

faqs.question: Is there an exam at the end of the Middle Years Programme in Dubai?
faqs.answer: It depends on the school. Some enter MYP 5 candidates for IB MYP eAssessment, which combines on-screen examinations and ePortfolios and leads to the IB MYP Certificate; others assess internally against criteria throughout and the Personal Project is the only hard-deadline component. Ask your school's MYP coordinator which applies, because it changes the whole final year. We do not publish IB session dates, since ibo.org blocks automated access and nothing in this project has been confirmed from the IB directly.

faqs.question: When should the Personal Project really be started in MYP 5?
faqs.answer: The goal, the success criteria and the resource list belong in the earliest weeks, and the process journal should become a fifteen-minute weekly habit from week one. The project is marked out of twenty-four across planning, applying skills and reflecting, at eight marks each, and all three depend on documentation written as the work happens. Projects in this catchment fail on documentation rather than on ambition, and reconstructed journals read exactly like reconstruction to a marker.

faqs.question: What is a Personal Project coach allowed to touch, and what has to stay the student's?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the useful help is early. A tutor can test whether a goal is achievable with the time and resources available, explain what each of the three criteria rewards, model how a journal entry is written, ask the questions that produce real reflection, and comment on a draft the student has written. A tutor cannot choose the goal, make the product or write the report. The school authenticates the work as the student's own, and a false authentication puts the student at risk, not the helper.

faqs.question: My daughter was put in standard rather than extended mathematics for MYP 4. Does that matter?
faqs.answer: It matters more than almost anything else in the programme. Extended mathematics is the realistic preparation for Diploma Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, and standard mathematics generally is not - the gap appears in the first term of Year 12 rather than at the point of choosing. If her investigating patterns criterion is solid and the placement rested on computational accuracy, that case is worth making, with a timed extended-level task marked against the descriptors as the evidence.

faqs.question: Will an MYP tutor come to our apartment in Al Sufouh or the Marina?
faqs.answer: Not from us. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; tutors attending a student's address is a service we run only in India. Every lesson here is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. For a younger Middle Years student, presence in the room has genuine value and in-home tutoring exists in this market at published rates of roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel inside the price. We would rather say that plainly than argue the point away.

faqs.question: Is it worth starting tutoring in MYP 1 or MYP 2?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, but rarely as subject tutoring. At eleven or twelve the highest-value support is usually approaches to learning - how to read a task sheet, how to plan backwards from a deadline, how to keep a record that is actually usable, how to interpret a criteria descriptor. That pays across all eight subject groups rather than one. Three weekly subject sessions at that age removes the unstructured time in which independent study habits form, and the criteria reward precisely those habits.

faqs.question: Why does my son get strong marks for his Design products but a low overall grade?
faqs.answer: Because the design cycle is marked on process rather than on the finished object. Inquiring and analysing, and developing ideas, both reward documented investigation and iteration - research into existing solutions, design specifications, multiple developed options, justified choices. A student who produces something impressive without documenting how they got there loses marks under two criteria while the product itself is only part of a third. The fix is documentation habits, which also transfer directly into the Personal Project.

faqs.question: How does the move from MYP 5 into the Diploma actually feel?
faqs.answer: The content continues; the framing changes completely. Students move from criterion-referenced tasks assessed against descriptors to published assessment weightings, external papers and percentage marks, and the first set of examination-style results can be disorienting even for strong students. Mathematics is usually the subject where the gap is real rather than presentational, particularly for students who took standard rather than extended. Six to eight summer sessions on mathematics and on how weighted assessment works is the best value available in this whole sequence.

faqs.question: What should I ask the MYP coordinator at a school tour in this belt?
faqs.answer: Four things. Whether the school enters MYP 5 candidates for eAssessment. When the internal Personal Project deadlines fall. Whether mathematics separates into standard and extended in MYP 4 and on what evidence the recommendation is made. And how many periods a week each subject group actually receives, because all eight run every year alongside the mandatory UAE subjects and the arithmetic is tight. The published KHDA inspection report answers a fifth question about teaching quality before you arrive.

faqs.question: We need help in three subject groups at once - is one tutor for all of them sensible?
faqs.answer: For approaches to learning, yes - organisation, task-sheet reading, backwards planning and criteria interpretation transfer across all eight subject groups, and one person can teach all of it. For subject-specific criteria, less so: processing and evaluating in sciences and investigating patterns in mathematics are different skills requiring different expertise. The practical answer is usually one person for the systems work and a specialist where a single named criterion needs lifting, sequenced rather than run in parallel.

faqs.question: Does the mandatory Arabic requirement apply to Middle Years students too?
faqs.answer: Yes, in full. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are required in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, so they sit alongside the eight Middle Years subject groups rather than inside them. KHDA requires separate classes for Arab and non-Arab students in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and schools must ensure teachers of those subjects hold appropriate KHDA approval. For the mandatory subjects, additional or different content needs prior Ministry of Education permission, which limits what any tutor may offer.

faqs.question: What if the criterion we need help with is in a subject you cannot cover?
faqs.answer: We tell you rather than putting a generalist on it. Some Middle Years requirements are genuinely thin - a specific arts discipline, a language acquisition phase, or a physical and health education written criterion. When that happens you get three straight answers: how long a match realistically takes, whether the approaches-to-learning work would address part of the problem, and whether the school's own department is the better route. No competitor page in this market discloses a coverage limit at all.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-knowledge-park.closingHeading: Start with the report, not with a subject
dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-knowledge-park.closingBody: If you are looking for an IB MYP tutor in Dubai Knowledge Park, send the report with the individual criterion scores and ask the school for the published grade boundaries. Ten minutes with those two documents usually identifies one criterion in one subject, which is the only kind of target the next report can measure. If your child is in MYP 5, tell us the school's internal Personal Project deadline as well, because the useful help there is early and the late version does not exist. The trial lesson and the consultation cost nothing.

intro.heading: What MYP tutoring is for, when there is no exam to revise for
paragraphs: Parents in LA Mer who have been through IGCSE with an older child arrive at MYP tutoring expecting the same conversation and find a different one. There is no past paper to work through. There is no mark scheme published by an awarding body. The grade on the report was produced by the class teacher, marking a task they designed, against four published criteria each scored from zero to eight. The question a tutor has to answer is therefore not how do we practise for the exam, but what is this student actually being judged on.

The answer is more specific than most families are told. Every MYP subject has four criteria, labelled A to D, and they are different in each subject group. In mathematics they are knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. In the sciences they are knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. In language and literature they are analysing, organising, producing text, and using language. A student who is strong on content and weak on criterion B in mathematics has a pattern-finding and justification problem, not a maths problem, and no amount of extra practice questions will move the mark.

That makes diagnosis the first and most valuable thing a tutor does. The raw material is the student's own returned tasks with the criterion marks on them, which is information most families have in a folder and have never read as a dataset. Three reports in, the pattern is usually unmistakeable: consistently high on A, consistently low on C, which in almost every subject group means the thinking is sound and the communication of it is not. That is a teachable, bounded problem.

Timing in LA Mer follows the same arithmetic as every other subject in this cluster. Schools serving the Jumeirah 1 shoreline finish between about 2:45pm and 3:30pm, the drive home down Jumeirah Beach Road takes the next half hour, and activity programmes run to roughly 6pm. MYP students are younger than Diploma students and tire earlier, so the useful window is narrower: a session after 8pm with a twelve-year-old is not a session. One well-placed hour, either at 4:45pm where the activity calendar allows or at 6:30pm where it does not, is the arrangement that works.

IB Gram teaches LA Mer families one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time and does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE, since home visits are offered only in India. For MYP that has a particular advantage: the criterion descriptors and the student's own marked task can be on screen side by side, which is how a student comes to understand what a six looks like compared with a four.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-la-mer.programmesIntro: LA Mer sits close to several schools running the IB continuum, where MYP is the five years before the Diploma rather than a standalone qualification. These are the programmes that shape MYP tutoring here.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups taught across five years: language and literature, language acquisition, individuals and societies, sciences, mathematics, arts, physical and health education, and design. Each subject is assessed against four criteria, each from zero to eight, with the totals converted to a grade from one to seven using published boundaries. Interdisciplinary units, approaches to learning and service as action run alongside.
