sections.heading: What MYP tutoring costs, and what to ask before paying
paragraphs: MYP requests sit mostly in the qualified-tutor band rather than the specialist one, because the work is criterion decoding and skill practice rather than examination technique at Higher Level. A qualified subject tutor working online in this market sits at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200.

Below that, budget online and university-student tutors advertise from around AED 45 to 150, with EdFlik publishing AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya AED 33 to 52. For straightforward homework support with a younger MYP student that can be reasonable value. It is less suited to criterion work, which needs someone who has read the descriptors and marked against them. Above that, subject specialists run AED 200 to 450 and above, with TutorChase publishing AED 270.

In-home visits are quoted at roughly AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel inside the price, Bestimate's range being AED 180 to 350 and independent home tutors advertising AED 200 to 500. Bestimate's monthly estimates for a weekly hour run AED 240 to 600 budget, AED 600 to 1,200 mid and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more specialist. For context, KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that Dubai private school fees would not rise for 2026-27.

The questions worth asking are specific to this programme. Have you taught the MYP, in which subject group, and at which year levels. Have you marked against the criteria. What will you do with a Personal Project, and what will you refuse to do. Do you hold the MoHRE private tuition work permit, which is granted free of charge for two years under Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and shows a two-working-day completion time on MoHRE's own service listing.

faqs.question: How should a Mudon parent read a mark of 5 out of 8 on a criterion?
faqs.answer: That the work demonstrated a particular described level of a particular skill, not that five eighths of the content was learned. Descriptors are written in bands, usually covering two marks each, and each band describes qualitatively different performance. Moving up a band means doing something different rather than doing the same thing better. Read the published descriptor the school used: the gap is almost always one verb, such as describing where the next band asks for analysis, and once named it is specific enough to practise.

faqs.question: Why does my son's MYP report show strong knowledge and a weak overall grade?
faqs.answer: Because knowledge is only one of four criteria. Criterion A is broadly about knowing and understanding across most subject groups, and it behaves most like a traditional test. The other three assess different things: investigating, communicating, evaluating, reflecting, depending on the group. A student can know the content well and still lose marks for not justifying a method, not using the subject's conventions, or not reflecting on what the work showed. The reported grade is a conversion of all four, so one weak criterion pulls it down.

faqs.question: Does the same criterion letter mean the same thing in every subject?
faqs.answer: No, and this is the single most common misunderstanding among parents new to the programme. Criterion A is broadly knowing and understanding in most groups, but Criterion B is investigating patterns in mathematics, inquiring and designing in sciences, organising in language and literature, and developing ideas in design. A parent who learns what B means in one subject and applies it to another will misread the report. Ask the school for the descriptors for each subject group; they are published and short.

faqs.question: Our daughter joined the MYP in Year 7 from a British primary. What usually goes wrong first?
faqs.answer: The first reporting cycle, almost universally. She arrives capable and finds that the tasks ask her to do things she has not been taught to do: justify a method, analyse how a text achieves an effect, evaluate rather than conclude. The content is rarely the problem. A Year 7 MYP class in this belt contains children from PYP schools who already know the vocabulary and children from British primaries who do not, and that unevenness explains most first reports. It closes within a term once the descriptors are explained.

faqs.question: Which MYP mathematics criterion loses the most marks?
faqs.answer: Investigating patterns, in most cases. It rewards generalising from specific cases, testing a general rule and justifying why it holds, which is a different activity from solving a problem correctly. Students who are strong at calculation often score well on knowing and understanding and poorly here, because they reach the answer and stop. The repair is practising the sequence explicitly: try several cases, state a conjecture, test it, then justify it. That is a habit rather than content, and it transfers to every future investigation task.

faqs.question: How should the Personal Project be approached from the start?
faqs.answer: By narrowing the goal and starting the journal on day one. The project is assessed on planning, applying skills, reflecting and the report, not on how impressive the product is, and families consistently invert that. A narrow, specific goal produces rich evidence; an ambitious one produces thin evidence and a rushed journal. Dated entries written while the work happens, recording decisions, difficulties and changes of direction, are what the criteria reward. A journal assembled at the end is visible to a supervisor and scores accordingly.

faqs.question: Is a tutor allowed to produce any part of the Personal Project?
faqs.answer: No, and the boundary matters because the project is authenticated by the school. A tutor can explain each criterion, interrogate the goal until it is achievable and assessable, ask the questions the descriptors imply, suggest journal habits, and give feedback on a report draft the student has written. A tutor must not plan the project, produce any part of the product, draft the report or write journal entries. The purpose of the project is the student's own learning, and an authenticity problem is a serious matter rather than a mark penalty.

faqs.question: Are MYP command terms the same as Diploma ones?
faqs.answer: Largely the same words with the same obligations, but they sit inside longer task instructions rather than at the start of an exam question, which makes them easier to skip. Describe wants features without reasons. Explain wants causes stated as a chain. Analyse wants a breakdown into parts and their relationships. Evaluate wants strengths, limitations and a judgement. The same drill works: cover the task, keep the command term, and ask what it obliges. Most students in Years 7 to 9 cannot do this at first and can within a fortnight.

faqs.question: Does the MYP have exams at the end?
faqs.answer: Not compulsorily. Some schools enter students for the optional eAssessments, which are externally marked on-screen examinations with an ePortfolio in some subjects and produce a formal qualification; many schools do not, and their final MYP grades are internal. Which applies changes the shape of the final year considerably and whether the student leaves with an external qualification to show a receiving sixth form. It is a direct question for the school, worth asking at an open day rather than assumed either way.

faqs.question: How hard is the step from the MYP into the IB Diploma?
faqs.answer: Smoother than any other route in assessment language and harder than expected in examination load. Criteria, command terms, internally assessed work and the expectation of justification all carry over, which is a genuine advantage over a student arriving from an unexamined IGCSE background. What does not carry over is sitting timed papers, because the MYP has little or no external examination. Students who have never worked under a clock find the first Diploma mock a shock. A few timed papers before Year 12 starts removes most of that.

faqs.question: We may move our child from an MYP school to an IGCSE school. What should we plan?
faqs.answer: Talk to both schools early and expect to bridge content. Crossing systems mid-phase is the hardest of the available moves: the content order differs, the receiving cohort has had a two-year build-up, and tiering decisions may already be made for that year group. The student usually arrives with stronger research and writing habits and specific content gaps. A planned bridging block before the move, aimed at those gaps in the subjects that are tiered, is the difference between a difficult term and a lost year.

faqs.question: Which schools near Mudon actually run the Middle Years Programme?
faqs.answer: Provision is thinner than IGCSE provision in this belt. The nearest continuum options are Fairgreen International School in The Sustainable City and GEMS International School Al Khail, with Nord Anglia International School Dubai further along Al Khail Road. Most schools immediately around Mudon, including Jebel Ali School in DAMAC Hills, GEMS Metropole in Motor City and South View School, run British curriculum through IGCSE. A family committed to the MYP therefore usually accepts a longer school run, which is worth factoring into any evening plan. Schools are named as context only.

faqs.question: How long should a session be for a Year 8 student?
faqs.answer: Often shorter than an hour, and we will say so even where it means a smaller booking. At this age attention rather than content is usually the limiting factor, especially after a long run back from Al Khail or The Sustainable City. Forty minutes of focused criterion work with the marked task open generally achieves more than sixty minutes that drifts. Two shorter sessions a week can also beat one long one, because the practice is distributed, and the slot can move within the evening at no cost.

faqs.question: Do the mandatory UAE subjects appear in MYP reporting?
faqs.answer: They appear on the timetable and in school reporting alongside the eight MYP subject groups, because every Dubai private school must teach Arabic, Islamic Education and social and moral studies whatever curriculum it is licensed for. KHDA's requirements were to be implemented from the start of the 2025-26 academic year, separate classes are required for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes are prohibited. Any support in these subjects works with the school's own material, since additional content needs prior Ministry permission.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-mudon.closingHeading: Send the report and one marked task
dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-mudon.closingBody: The quickest way to make an MYP report useful is to put it beside the actual marked task and the published descriptor. Send both, with the subject group, the year level and the school, and a free trial lesson over live video is arranged before any payment is taken. The session should end with your child able to say, in their own words, what the next band asks for. Lessons are delivered online on Gulf Standard Time, in session lengths that suit the age, and home visits are a service IB Gram runs in India only.

intro.heading: Why a good subject tutor can be useless in the MYP
paragraphs: A parent in Muhaisnah searching for Middle Years Programme support is usually reacting to a report that makes no sense. There are no percentages. There are letters with numbers beside them: criterion A, 5; criterion C, 4. There is a subject grade out of 7 that seems to have arrived from nowhere. And there is a comment about inquiry and conceptual understanding that gives no indication of what to do on Tuesday evening. The instinct is to hire a tutor for the subject, and that instinct is frequently wrong.

The reason is that the Middle Years Programme does not assess content the way the systems most tutors trained in do. Each subject has four criteria, each marked from 0 to 8 against published descriptors, and the four are summed and converted to a grade from 1 to 7 using published boundaries. The criteria are different in each subject group. In sciences they are knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. In mathematics they are knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts.

Read those again and notice what they are not. Only one of the four in each case is about knowing the content. The other three are about designing an investigation, communicating a process, applying an idea in an unfamiliar context, or evaluating consequences. A student with excellent content knowledge who writes terse answers, skips process description and never addresses the real-life application criterion will sit at 4 or 5 and no amount of additional content teaching will move them. That is the single most common situation we are called about from this catchment.

Which is why the verification question for an MYP tutor is specific rather than general. Ask them to name the four criteria for your child's subject, and to explain how a criterion total becomes a 1-7 grade. A tutor who genuinely teaches the programme answers in forty seconds. A good subject tutor who has never taught it will describe topics, which tells you they will prepare your child for an examination that does not exist.

Muhaisnah makes this harder in the usual way. The schools nearest this neighbourhood are predominantly Indian and British curriculum, so local tutoring supply reflects that, and continuum provision sits further out in Mirdif, Festival City and Nad Al Sheba. An MYP specialist is not somebody who happens to live nearby. IB Gram does not send tutors to UAE addresses in any case: home visiting is a service we run only in India, and for Muhaisnah families every lesson is one-to-one over live video at a Gulf Standard Time slot, with a free trial lesson before anything is charged.

Only one criterion in each subject group is primarily about content knowledge
The criteria differ by subject group, so a tutor must know the right four
Grades reflect most recent and most consistent achievement, not an average
The Personal Project in the final year is marked out of 24 across three criteria

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-muhaisnah.programmesIntro: The Middle Years Programme runs five years and the tutoring job changes substantially across them. These are the stages Muhaisnah families contact us about.

programmes.name: Middle Years, the first three years
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each assessed against its own four criteria at least twice a year. Interdisciplinary units run alongside. Assessment is criterion-referenced throughout, with task-specific clarifications published by the teacher for each task so students know what the descriptors mean in context.
programmes.countryNote: This is where the habits form and where support is cheapest and most effective. A student in Year 8 who learns to read a task-specific clarification and write deliberately against it carries that skill through to the Diploma. The slots are also uncontested: a half past five session is realistic at this age.

programmes.name: Middle Years, the final two years
programmes.description: Deeper subject work with some schools offering extended and standard mathematics routes, plus the Personal Project in the final year and continued service as action. Some schools enter students for MYP eAssessment, which involves on-screen examinations and ePortfolios leading to an IB MYP Certificate.
programmes.countryNote: The most common point of contact from this catchment, usually because a student's grades have slipped or the Personal Project has stalled. Both are tractable, but the Personal Project in particular has a hard deadline and a supervisor in school, so the tutoring has to work alongside that process rather than around it.

programmes.name: The Personal Project
programmes.description: An independent project of the student's own choosing, supervised in school, assessed against three criteria marked out of 8 each: planning, applying skills, and reflecting. The process journal matters as much as the product, because the criteria reward the documented process rather than the finished object.
programmes.countryNote: The commonest Personal Project failure we see from eastern Dubai is a student with an impressive product and a thin process journal, who is then surprised by the mark. The journal is the evidence, and a tutor's most useful intervention is making that clear in month one rather than month five.

programmes.name: The transition into the Diploma
programmes.description: The shift from criterion-referenced internal assessment to externally examined papers with sustained written answers under time pressure. Content continuity is good; assessment continuity is poor, and students who were strong on process criteria can find the first Diploma papers a shock.
programmes.countryNote: Families in Mirdif and Festival City continuum schools often ask us whether their child is ready for the Diploma. The useful answer is subject by subject, based on which criteria they score well on, and the honest one is that by-hand fluency and timed performance are the two things the Middle Years Programme does not push.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-muhaisnah.subjectsIntro: Each MYP subject group has its own four criteria. These are the groups Muhaisnah enquiries name, with the criterion that most often holds a student back.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.levels: Standard and extended routes in MYP 4-5
subjects.description: Criteria are knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Students with fluent arithmetic lose marks on investigating patterns, where they find the rule and never justify or generalise it.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.levels: Integrated, then subject-specific in some schools
subjects.description: Criteria are knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. Inquiring and designing is the usual gap: a hypothesis without a reason, or variables identified loosely.

subjects.name: Language and literature
subjects.description: Criteria are analysing, organizing, producing text, and using language. Students write about what a text says rather than how it works, which caps analysing, and under-plan, which caps organizing. Both respond quickly to being taught deliberately.

subjects.name: Language acquisition
subjects.description: Criteria cover listening, reading, speaking and writing, and students are placed in a phase rather than a year group. A student placed in too high a phase will score poorly on everything, which is a placement question for the school rather than a tutoring one.

subjects.name: Individuals and societies
subjects.description: Criteria are knowing and understanding, investigating, communicating, and thinking critically. Thinking critically is where marks sit and where students substitute description for evaluation, which is a teachable distinction rather than a maturity one.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: Criteria are inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution, and evaluating. Students build competent products and document thinly, which is the same failure pattern as the Personal Project and for the same reason.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.description: Criteria are knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively, and responding. The process portfolio carries a substantial share of the marks, and students who make without documenting are penalised for something they could easily have avoided.

subjects.name: Physical and health education
subjects.description: Criteria are knowing and understanding, planning for performance, applying and performing, and reflecting and improving performance. The written and planning criteria surprise families who assume the subject is assessed on physical ability.

subjects.name: Interdisciplinary units
subjects.description: Assessed against interdisciplinary criteria rather than a single subject's. Students treat them as a side activity and lose marks that count, because the grade reported is a real one and the synthesis demanded is genuinely different.

subjects.name: The Personal Project
subjects.description: Three criteria marked out of 8: planning, applying skills, reflecting. Twenty-four marks in total, with the process journal rather than the product carrying the evidence. Starting the journal late is the most common and most expensive error.

subjects.name: Approaches to learning skills
subjects.description: Communication, social, self-management, research and thinking skills, taught explicitly and assessed implicitly through the subject criteria. Weak self-management shows up as low criterion scores in subjects where the content was never the problem.

subjects.name: Service as action
subjects.description: Required participation with reflection, not a graded subject. Reflection quality is what the school records, and students who treat it as attendance miss the point and sometimes the requirement.

sections.heading: What the Middle Years Programme actually assesses
paragraphs: The Middle Years Programme has eight subject groups: language and literature, language acquisition, individuals and societies, sciences, mathematics, arts, physical and health education, and design. Each group is assessed against four criteria, each marked from 0 to 8 against published descriptors, and teachers publish task-specific clarifications so students know what a descriptor means for a particular piece of work. At least one interdisciplinary unit runs each year, assessed against its own criteria.

The criteria are also different in each subject group, and only one of the four in each case is primarily about knowing content. The rest reward investigation, communication, application in unfamiliar contexts and critical evaluation. A student can therefore be knowledgeable and mid-band simultaneously, which is the situation that brings most Muhaisnah families to a tutoring search in the first place.

Grades are reported from 1 to 7, derived from the criterion total out of 32 using published boundary tables. The judgement is based on the most recent and most consistent achievement rather than on an average of everything the student has produced, which means a poor task in September does not permanently weigh down a grade and a strong task in September does not protect it. Families from averaging systems find this counterintuitive and it is worth understanding, because it changes which work matters.

The table sets out the groups with their criteria and the one that most commonly holds students back in our experience of this catchment. Use it to read your child's report properly: find the criterion with the lowest mark, then ask the teacher for the task-specific clarification for the task it came from. That single request, which costs nothing, frequently makes a tutoring booking unnecessary.

sections.heading: From criterion marks to a grade out of 7
paragraphs: This is where most of the confusion in a Muhaisnah household sits. A report shows criterion marks out of 8 and a subject grade out of 7, and the relationship between them is not obvious. The four criterion marks are summed, giving a total out of 32, and that total is converted to a grade from 1 to 7 using boundary tables the school applies. The boundaries are published, so the school can tell you exactly what total your child's grade required.

That arithmetic has a practical consequence families can act on. The cheapest grade movement available is usually not in the criterion the student is worst at, but in the one where the gap between their current mark and the next descriptor band is smallest. Moving a 4 to a 5 on a communication criterion by learning to label, structure and justify is often a two-week job. Moving a 3 to a 5 on a critical-thinking criterion is a term's work. Both add the same amount to the total.

The second consequence concerns which tasks matter. Because the judgement rests on most recent and most consistent achievement, the tasks late in the year carry more weight than the ones early in it. A student who has a poor first term and a strong second should see that reflected, and a student who did well in September and drifted should expect the opposite. Parents who understand this stop treating an early report as a verdict.

The table below shows the mechanism with worked examples rather than in the abstract. It is deliberately not a boundary table, because boundaries are published by the IB and applied by the school and we are not going to reproduce them: ask your child's school for the ones they use. What the table shows is how different distributions of criterion marks behave, and why the lowest criterion is not always the one to work on.

sections.heading: The Personal Project: three criteria, 24 marks, and a journal
paragraphs: In the final Middle Years year every student completes a Personal Project: an independent piece of work of their own choosing, supervised by a member of staff, assessed against three criteria each marked out of 8. Those criteria are planning, applying skills, and reflecting, giving a total of 24. The product can be almost anything. What is assessed is the process, documented.

The failure pattern from this catchment is consistent and avoidable. A student picks something ambitious, works hard on it, produces something genuinely impressive, and keeps almost no record of their thinking. The product is not what earns the marks. The planning criterion rewards a clear goal with criteria for success set in advance; applying skills rewards evidence of the approaches-to-learning skills actually used; reflecting rewards analysis of the impact of the project and of the student's own learning. All three need written evidence as the work happens.

So the highest-value intervention is in the first month, not the fifth. One session establishing what the process journal must contain and how often it must be updated protects most of the available marks. By the time a parent realises the journal is thin, usually weeks before the deadline, the evidence for a process that happened months earlier can no longer be honestly created, and manufacturing it retrospectively is not available as an option.

The boundary here is firm and worth stating. A tutor may explain what each criterion asks for, question whether the goal is achievable, ask what success criteria the student has set, interrogate the quality of reflection, and read the student's own journal and say which descriptor is not yet met. A tutor may not plan the project, build the product, write the journal or compose the reflection. The school's supervisor owns the formal process, and the most useful session before a supervisor meeting is often rehearsing the questions the student will be asked about their own work.

sections.heading: eAssessment: what it is and whether it applies to your child
paragraphs: Some schools enter final-year Middle Years students for IB MYP eAssessment, which produces an externally validated IB MYP Certificate. It involves on-screen examinations in several subjects and ePortfolios in others, and it is optional at the school level, so a student in one Dubai continuum school may sit it while a student in another does not. Ask your school directly; the answer changes what the final year looks like substantially.

If your child is sitting eAssessment, the final Middle Years year contains something closer to an examination than the rest of the programme does, and the preparation required is partly conventional: timed practice, familiarity with the on-screen format, and the discipline of producing a sustained written answer in a fixed window. That is a different kind of work from criterion coaching and should be planned as a separate, bounded block.

If your child is not sitting eAssessment, there is no terminal examination in the Middle Years Programme at all, and any tutor proposing exam revision has misunderstood the programme. The work is on assessed tasks against criteria, continuously, which means the tutoring should be timed to the school's assessment calendar rather than to a revision season. Ask the school when the next assessed task in the weak criterion falls, and aim the support at that.

This distinction is also a useful tutor test. Ask whether eAssessment applies to your child's school and what it would involve. A tutor who knows the programme will ask you which school and whether it enters students, because they know it varies. A tutor who answers confidently either way without asking is guessing, and the guess tells you how familiar they are with how the programme is actually run in Dubai.

sections.heading: The Middle Years to Diploma gap, subject by subject
paragraphs: Families in Mirdif and Festival City continuum schools ask us regularly whether their child is ready for the Diploma, and the honest answer is subject by subject rather than overall. Content continuity between the programmes is good; assessment continuity is poor. A student who has spent five years producing criterion-marked tasks with planning time, resources available and a chance to redraft meets a Diploma paper that wants a sustained argument produced from memory in forty minutes.

The two specific gaps are consistent. First, by-hand fluency, particularly in mathematics and the sciences, because the Middle Years Programme permits technology more freely and does not drill speed. Second, timed sustained writing, because criterion tasks reward completeness and process while Diploma papers reward selection under pressure. Neither gap is a reflection of the student's ability, and both are closeable in a bounded block before the Diploma begins.

There is also a diagnostic opportunity in the criterion marks themselves, which almost nobody uses. A student who consistently scores well on knowing and understanding but poorly on investigating or critical thinking will find the Diploma's internal assessments harder than its papers. A student with the reverse profile will find the papers harder than the internal assessments. Either way, the criterion pattern predicts which part of the Diploma will need support, which is far more useful than a single grade.

The table below sets out the transition subject by subject with the specific gap and the useful preparation. The right time for this work is the summer between the programmes or the first term of the Diploma, and the right size is a short block rather than a year-long slot. Families who do it report a much smoother first term, and families who do not generally ask us for help in November.

sections.heading: Forty seconds that reveal whether a tutor knows the programme
paragraphs: Two questions, in this order, on any tutor including ours. First: name the four criteria for my child's subject in the Middle Years Programme. Second: explain how those criterion marks become the grade out of 7 on the report. A tutor who teaches the programme answers both in well under a minute. A subject tutor who has not will describe topics or talk generally about continuous assessment.

If you want a third, ask what a task-specific clarification is and whether they would want to see one. The right answer is yes, immediately, because the clarification is how a published descriptor is translated into expectations for a particular task, and working without it means guessing at what the teacher is marking against. A tutor who has never heard the term has not taught the programme, whatever their subject credentials.

A fourth, if you have a report in front of you: look at these criterion marks and tell me which one we should work on, and why. The interesting part is the why. A good answer identifies the smallest descriptor gap rather than the lowest number, and explains that both add the same amount to the total. An answer that simply points at the lowest mark is not wrong but it is not informed by how the grade is built.

The reason these questions matter more in this programme than anywhere else is that the Middle Years Programme has no examination to fall back on. In an IGCSE subject, a tutor who knows the content but not the paper still delivers something useful. In the Middle Years Programme, a tutor who does not know the criteria is teaching towards an assessment that does not exist, and the student's marks will not move however good the teaching is.

sections.heading: Why "revision" is the wrong word for this programme
paragraphs: Parents arriving from systems with terminal examinations naturally ask for revision, and in the Middle Years Programme there is usually nothing to revise for. Unless the school enters students for eAssessment, there is no terminal paper. The grade is built from assessed tasks across the year, each marked against criteria, and the way to improve it is to produce better tasks rather than to recall more content before a date.

That changes the shape of useful support. It should be timed to the school's assessment calendar: ask when the next assessed task in the weak criterion falls, and aim the work at that. It should use the student's own returned tasks as material, because the teacher's comments and the criterion marks are the most specific diagnostic available. And it should be aimed at a descriptor rather than at a topic, which is a different kind of lesson from the one most tutors default to.

It also changes what to ask of your child. Not "have you revised" but "what does criterion C want on this task, and where in your draft have you done it". If they cannot answer, the task-specific clarification is the document to find, and the teacher will supply it. That conversation costs nothing and in a meaningful number of cases resolves the problem without any tutoring at all, which we would rather tell you than not.

Finally, the approaches-to-learning skills deserve a mention here because they are where a surprising number of criterion losses originate. Communication, social, self-management, research and thinking skills are taught explicitly in the programme and assessed implicitly through the subject criteria. A student with weak self-management produces late, unplanned work that scores poorly on organising and communicating in every subject at once. That is one problem presenting as six, and treating it as six subject problems is both expensive and ineffective.

sections.heading: Starting Middle Years support from Muhaisnah
paragraphs: Send three things. The most recent report with the criterion marks visible, which is the real diagnostic. One or two of the student's own returned assessed tasks with the teacher's comments. And the task-specific clarification for the task where the lowest criterion mark came from, which the teacher will provide if you ask.

With those three a specialist can tell you within a session whether this is a criterion-literacy problem, a content problem, an approaches-to-learning problem or a placement problem, and the four need completely different responses. Placement is worth naming separately: a language acquisition student in too high a phase will score poorly on every criterion, and no tutoring fixes a placement question that belongs with the school.

Expect the match to take a little longer than for a mainstream subject. Genuine Middle Years specialists are thinner on the ground than Diploma or IGCSE subject tutors, particularly for design, arts and language acquisition, and the specialist may be based outside the UAE teaching at a Gulf Standard Time slot. We will tell you the wait rather than offering a subject tutor who will learn the programme on your child's time.

Then agree one narrow target tied to the next assessed task. Not "improve in science" but "write an inquiry question with a reasoned hypothesis and three tightly defined variables, unprompted". You check it on the returned task, against the criterion mark, which makes the review evidence rather than conversation. And if the answer turns out to be a free one-hour conversation with the subject teacher, we would rather say so than take the booking.

process.title: Send the report with criterion marks
process.description: The criterion marks out of 8, not the grade out of 7, are the diagnostic. They say whether the student is losing marks on content, on process, on communication or on critical thinking, and those four need entirely different work.

process.title: Send a returned task and its clarification
process.description: One or two of the student's own assessed tasks with the teacher's comments, plus the task-specific clarification for the lowest-scoring criterion. The teacher will supply the clarification if you ask, and it is the document a specialist works from.

process.title: Expect a realistic match time
process.description: Genuine Middle Years specialists are thinner than Diploma or IGCSE subject tutors, particularly in design, arts and language acquisition. We will state the wait rather than offering a subject tutor who learns the programme on your child's time.

process.title: Test the tutor in forty seconds
process.description: Ask them to name the four criteria for the subject and explain how criterion marks become a grade out of 7. A programme tutor answers both in under a minute; a subject tutor describes topics. The free trial exists for exactly this.

process.title: Aim at the next assessed task
process.description: Ask the school when the next assessed task in the weak criterion falls and aim the work at that date. There is nothing to revise for in this programme unless eAssessment applies, so support follows the assessment calendar.

process.title: Review on the returned task
process.description: One narrow capability, checked against the criterion mark on the next returned task. Continue, change the tutor, change the diagnosis or stop. If a conversation with the subject teacher would have done it, we would rather have said so.

whyPoints.title: Criteria tested before subject knowledge
whyPoints.description: A tutor is asked to name the four criteria for the subject and explain the conversion to a grade out of 7 before a booking is confirmed. In a programme with no terminal examination, a tutor who does not know the criteria is teaching towards an assessment that does not exist.

whyPoints.title: Work built on the school's own clarifications
whyPoints.description: Task-specific clarifications are how published descriptors become expectations for a particular task. We ask for them and work from them, because without one a tutor is guessing at what the teacher is marking against.

whyPoints.title: The cheapest gain, not the lowest mark
whyPoints.description: Because criterion marks are summed, a point gained on a communication criterion counts the same as one gained on critical thinking and often takes a fortnight rather than a term. We aim at the smallest descriptor gap rather than the worst number.

whyPoints.title: Process journal treated as the assessment
whyPoints.description: The Personal Project is marked on documented process rather than on the product, which is why the useful intervention is in month one. We will not plan, build, write or reflect on a student's behalf at any price.

whyPoints.title: One problem, not six
whyPoints.description: Weak self-management produces late, unplanned work that scores poorly on organising and communicating in every subject simultaneously. We look for that pattern before recommending subject tutoring, because six subject bookings is the expensive way to treat one issue.

whyPoints.title: We will send you back to the teacher
whyPoints.description: A free conversation with the subject teacher, armed with the task-specific clarification, resolves a meaningful share of the cases that reach us. Saying so costs a booking and is the honest answer more often than this market admits.

faqs.question: Why does my child's MYP report have no percentages?
faqs.answer: Because the Middle Years Programme is criterion-referenced rather than mark-based. Each subject is assessed against four criteria, each from 0 to 8 against published descriptors, and the four are summed to a total out of 32 which converts to a grade from 1 to 7 using boundary tables the school applies. There is no percentage anywhere in the system. Families arriving from systems that report out of 100 commonly misread a 5 out of 8 as a near-failure when it may be a solid, mid-to-upper band performance against that descriptor.

faqs.question: Can a good subject tutor help with the Middle Years Programme?
faqs.answer: Only partly, and the gap matters more here than in any examined course. Each subject group has its own four criteria and typically only one of them is primarily about knowing content; the rest reward designing an inquiry, communicating a process, applying ideas in unfamiliar contexts or evaluating critically. A tutor who teaches content will help a student who has a content gap and will not move a student losing marks on the other three criteria. Ask any candidate to name the four criteria for your child's subject before booking.

faqs.question: My child knows the material but sits at a 4 or 5. What is going on?
faqs.answer: Almost always the process criteria. In sciences, a hypothesis stated without a reason and variables identified loosely cap inquiring and designing. In mathematics, finding a pattern and never justifying or generalising it caps investigating patterns. In language and literature, writing about what a text says rather than how it works caps analysing. None of these is a knowledge problem, all of them are teachable within weeks, and none of them responds to more content coverage, which is what most tutoring defaults to.

faqs.question: How do criterion marks out of 8 turn into a grade out of 7?
faqs.answer: The four criterion marks are summed to a total out of 32, and that total converts to a grade from 1 to 7 using published boundary tables the school applies. Ask your school what total your child's grade required; they can tell you exactly. The useful consequence is that a point gained anywhere counts the same, so the cheapest improvement is usually in the criterion with the smallest gap to the next descriptor band rather than in the one with the lowest number.

faqs.question: What is a task-specific clarification and why do you want it?
faqs.answer: It is the document in which a teacher translates the published criterion descriptors into expectations for one particular task. Without it, both student and tutor are guessing at what the marking will look for, which is why a tutor who has never heard the term has not taught this programme. Ask the subject teacher for the clarification covering the task where your child's lowest criterion mark came from. It is free, it is specific, and in a meaningful number of cases reading it with your child resolves the issue without tutoring.

faqs.question: Is the Personal Project marked on what my child makes?
faqs.answer: No, and this surprises most families. It is assessed against three criteria, each out of 8: planning, applying skills and reflecting, giving 24 marks in total. The evidence is the documented process, principally the process journal, not the finished product. The commonest failure in this catchment is an impressive product with a thin journal, discovered weeks before the deadline when the evidence for work done months earlier can no longer honestly be produced. One session in month one protects most of the marks.

faqs.question: Where exactly does a tutor stop on the Personal Project?
faqs.answer: A tutor may explain what each criterion asks for, question whether the goal is achievable, ask what success criteria the student has set in advance, interrogate the quality of reflection, and read the student's own journal to say which descriptor is not yet met. A tutor may not plan the project, build the product, write the journal or compose the reflection. The school allocates a supervisor who owns the formal process, and the most useful preparation before a supervisor meeting is rehearsing the questions the student will be asked about their own work.

faqs.question: Does my child sit exams at the end of the Middle Years Programme?
faqs.answer: Only if the school enters students for IB MYP eAssessment, which is optional at school level and produces an externally validated IB MYP Certificate through on-screen examinations and ePortfolios. Ask your school directly, because practice varies between Dubai continuum schools. If eAssessment does not apply, there is no terminal examination at all and any tutor proposing exam revision has misunderstood the programme. If it does apply, that preparation is a separate bounded block from criterion coaching.

faqs.question: Which MYP subjects are hardest to find a tutor for?
faqs.answer: Design, the arts and language acquisition, by a clear margin, and the reason is that each has criteria unlike anything in an examined curriculum. Design is assessed on inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution and evaluating, which almost no subject tutor outside the programme has worked with. Language acquisition places students in phases rather than year groups, which changes what good looks like. Expect a longer match for these and expect the specialist to be based outside the UAE teaching at a Gulf Standard Time slot.

faqs.question: My child moved from CBSE into the Middle Years Programme and the grades dropped. Is that normal?
faqs.answer: Very, and it is the commonest transition story in this catchment. A student arriving with strong content meets an assessment model that awards most of its marks for process, design, communication and evaluation. They answer correctly, briefly, and score mid-band, which looks like a decline in ability and is actually a change in what is being measured. The adjustment takes roughly a term when it is taught deliberately and considerably longer when nobody explains it. Start with the criterion marks and the task-specific clarifications rather than with content.

faqs.question: Will the Middle Years Programme prepare my child for the Diploma?
faqs.answer: Well on content and conceptual understanding, less well on two specific things: by-hand fluency without technology, particularly in mathematics and the sciences, and sustained writing from memory under time pressure. Both are closeable in a bounded block in the summer before the Diploma or in its first term. The criterion pattern is also a useful predictor: a student strong on knowing and understanding but weak on investigating will find the Diploma's internal assessments harder than its papers, and vice versa.

faqs.question: Is there an MYP tutor living near Muhaisnah?
faqs.answer: Unlikely, and the reason is the local school mix rather than the search. The schools closest to Muhaisnah are predominantly Indian and British curriculum, so the neighbourhood's tutoring supply reflects that; continuum provision sits further out in Mirdif, Festival City and Nad Al Sheba. An advertised MYP tutor here is frequently a subject tutor who has heard of the programme. IB Gram does not send tutors to UAE addresses in any case, and matches on criterion knowledge rather than proximity, teaching one-to-one over live video.

faqs.question: How often should Middle Years sessions run?
faqs.answer: Weekly is normal, and the timing should follow the school's assessment calendar rather than a fixed pattern. Ask when the next assessed task in the weak criterion falls and aim the work at that date, because there is no revision season to work towards unless eAssessment applies. For younger students, two shorter sessions beat one long one: a twenty-five minute slot twice a week suits a Year 7 after a long bus journey far better than ninety minutes once.

faqs.question: Could my child's problem be one thing showing up in several subjects?
faqs.answer: Frequently, and it is worth checking before booking anything. The approaches-to-learning skills, communication, social, self-management, research and thinking, are taught explicitly and assessed implicitly through the subject criteria. A student with weak self-management produces late, unplanned work that scores poorly on organising and communicating in every subject at once. That is one problem presenting as six, and six subject bookings is an expensive and ineffective way to treat it. Look for the same criterion scoring low across unrelated subjects.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-muhaisnah.closingHeading: Ask for the criteria, then for the clarification
dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-muhaisnah.closingBody: Two free steps come before any tutoring decision in this programme. Find the lowest criterion mark on your child's report, then ask the subject teacher for the task-specific clarification covering the task it came from. Read it with your child and ask them to show you where in their work that criterion was served. If they can, the problem is content. If they cannot, you have found it, and we can help. Send us the report, a returned task and the clarification, and we will match a tutor who knows the criteria and offer a free trial lesson. Nothing is charged before it.

intro.heading: A report nobody explains, and five years that decide the Diploma
paragraphs: The Middle Years Programme runs across eight subject groups: language and literature, language acquisition, individuals and societies, sciences, mathematics, arts, physical and health education, and design. Each subject is assessed against four criteria, each criterion carries a level from zero to eight, and the four are combined to a total out of thirty-two which converts to a grade from one to seven using published boundaries. That is the whole machinery, and almost no school explains it to parents in a form they can act on.

The reason it matters is that the four criteria measure different things, and a student can be strong on two and weak on two while receiving a middling overall grade that reveals nothing. A science student who knows the content thoroughly and cannot design an investigation will show a high level on knowing and understanding and a low one on inquiring and designing. The remedy for that student is not more science. It is three sessions on experimental design, and the report already said so to anyone who could read it.

The second thing the programme does, quietly, is set up the Diploma. Two MYP decisions carry forward with real force. The first is standard or extended mathematics in MYP 4 and 5, which largely determines whether Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is realistic two years later. The second is whether a student has ever genuinely produced long-form independent work, which the Personal Project in MYP 5 is designed to force and which predicts how the Extended Essay and the internal assessments will go.

The calendar inside MYP is gentler than the Diploma's but it is not empty. MYP 5 carries the Personal Project with school-set deadlines across the year, and in schools that run eAssessment it carries on-screen examinations and ePortfolios leading to the MYP Certificate. The years before that carry the gradual accumulation of the skills those tasks assess, which is why MYP support bought in MYP 3 or 4 is worth more per hour than the same money spent in a panic in MYP 5.

Nad Al Hamar is a residential district on the eastern side of Dubai, between the Ras Al Khor sanctuary and the Dubai-Al Ain Road. There is no school inside the district, and MYP children travel out to the IB continuum schools in Mirdif and the Festival City cluster, reaching home between about 3.50pm and 4.35pm. Teaching is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE, because home tutoring is a service we run in India only. For a younger student the practical consequence is that sessions should be shorter and earlier than a Diploma student's, which the online format makes easy to arrange.

programmes.name: Years 7 to 9
programmes.description: The years in which criteria-based habits are formed: justifying an answer, investigating a pattern rather than computing one, communicating with correct terminology, and applying a concept to an unfamiliar context. Support here is cheap, infrequent and compounds, because every later assessment in both MYP and the Diploma rewards the same habits.

programmes.name: Years 10 and 11
programmes.description: Subject choices narrow, mathematics splits into standard and extended, and MYP 5 carries the Personal Project. Schools running eAssessment add on-screen examinations and ePortfolios leading to the MYP Certificate. This is the stretch where a vague report becomes consequential, because the Diploma subject and level choices are made at the end of it.

programmes.name: MYP 5 into DP1
programmes.description: The step is in volume of independent work and in the shift from criterion descriptors to mark schemes. A student used to being rewarded for process meets papers that reward precise answers and specific command terms. Six to eight weeks of bridging work, particularly in mathematics and the sciences, removes most of the first-term difficulty.
programmes.countryNote: Families here often travel for a long summer, which makes bridging work awkward in person and straightforward over video across time zones. For a student moving from MYP standard mathematics into any Diploma mathematics course, this block is the single highest-value purchase in the sequence.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-nad-al-hamar.subjectsIntro: The eight MYP subject groups, with the criterion that most often causes the trouble in each.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Four criteria, with investigating patterns the one that separates students. It asks for generalisation from specific cases, which is a different activity from calculating, and it is the criterion that predicts Diploma readiness more reliably than any overall grade.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. Inquiring and designing is where content-strong students lose levels, because designing a fair test is a skill nobody teaches them directly.

subjects.name: Language and literature
subjects.description: Analysing, organising, producing text, and using language. Organising is the common gap: students have ideas and present them without a structure that the reader can follow, which costs levels across every task in the subject.

subjects.name: Language acquisition
subjects.description: Listening, reading, speaking and writing, assessed by phase rather than by age, which confuses parents comparing children in the same year. Progress depends on exposure volume more than on explanation, which shapes what tutoring can usefully do.

subjects.name: Individuals and societies
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, investigating, communicating, and thinking critically. Thinking critically is the criterion that rewards evaluating a source rather than summarising it, and it is the direct ancestor of Diploma essay marks in history and economics.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: Inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution, and evaluating. Heavily process-driven: students who build something good and document the process thinly score far below what the product suggests.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively, and responding. The process journal carries more weight than students expect, and a strong performer who keeps no record of development loses levels on two criteria out of four.

subjects.name: Physical and health education
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, planning for performance, applying and performing, and reflecting and improving performance. Written and reflective components exist and are frequently neglected by students who assume the subject is entirely practical.

subjects.name: The Personal Project
subjects.description: Assessed against its own criteria, covering planning, applying skills and reflecting, each marked out of eight. The process journal and the reflection carry a large share, and the quality of the product matters less than students and parents assume.

sections.heading: Reading an MYP report so it tells you what to do
paragraphs: An MYP report gives four criterion levels per subject, each from zero to eight, and an overall grade from one to seven derived from their total out of thirty-two. Parents read the grade and stop, which is understandable and loses most of the information. The grade is a summary; the four levels are a diagnosis. Two students with the same grade can need entirely different interventions, and the report already distinguishes them.

The pattern to look for is unevenness. A science student at level seven on knowing and understanding and level three on inquiring and designing is not weak at science. They have never been taught to design a fair test, which is a specific, teachable, four-session problem. A language and literature student strong on analysing and weak on organising has ideas and no structure, which is also specific and also quick. A mathematics student strong on knowing and understanding and weak on investigating patterns is fluent and cannot generalise, and that one matters most because it predicts the Diploma.

Even levels across all four tell a different story. A student at level four on everything is not hiding a specific gap; they are performing consistently at a middling standard, and that responds to subject teaching rather than to criterion work. A student at level seven on everything needs extension rather than support, and the honest advice to their parents is often to spend the money elsewhere.

The second thing to look for is movement between reporting periods. A level that has fallen is more informative than a level that is low, because something changed. Usually it is the task type: a student who scored well on a structured task and poorly on an open investigation has met a criterion they cannot yet access. That is the conversation to have with the subject teacher, and it is a more productive one than asking generally how the child is doing.

sections.heading: The four criteria in each subject group, named
paragraphs: Each MYP subject group has its own four criteria, and they are not interchangeable between subjects. This is the single most useful page of information a parent of an MYP student can hold, because it converts a report into a vocabulary the school will recognise. Asking a teacher how to raise criterion B in sciences is a different and far more productive conversation than asking how to improve at science.

In mathematics the four are knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. In sciences they are knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. In language and literature they are analysing, organising, producing text, and using language. In individuals and societies they are knowing and understanding, investigating, communicating, and thinking critically.

In language acquisition the four map onto listening, reading, speaking and writing, assessed by phase rather than by year group, which is the usual source of confusion when parents compare two children of the same age in different phases. In design they are inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution, and evaluating. In arts they are knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively, and responding. In physical and health education they are knowing and understanding, planning for performance, applying and performing, and reflecting and improving performance.

The practical pattern across all eight groups is that two of the four criteria in each subject reward process and documentation rather than performance. Students who are good at the subject and poor at recording what they did lose levels in every group, and it is the commonest systematic underperformance in the programme. It is also among the easiest things to fix, because it is a habit rather than an ability.

sections.heading: The MYP 5 year, and what eAssessment adds
paragraphs: MYP 5 is the year with structure, and families are often surprised by how much of it is deadline-driven. The Personal Project runs across the whole year with school-set checkpoints. Subject assessment continues against the criteria. And in schools that offer it, eAssessment adds on-screen examinations and ePortfolios that lead to the formal MYP Certificate. Not every IB school runs eAssessment, so the first question is whether yours does, because the year looks materially different either way.

Where eAssessment runs, the on-screen examinations reward something the Diploma papers do not: a strong emphasis on process, justification and the application of concepts to unfamiliar material, assessed in a digital format. A student can do well in these and still be underprepared for Diploma papers, which reward precise answers to specific command terms. That mismatch is worth knowing in advance, because a strong MYP 5 result can create false confidence going into DP1.

The autumn term of MYP 5 is the useful window for anything structural: criterion habits, the Personal Project proposal, and the standard-or-extended mathematics decision if it is still open. By the spring the Personal Project is due and the examinations are close, and the honest work is finishing what exists rather than starting anything. A parent reading this in the autumn has options that a parent reading it in April does not.

One practical note on the certificate. The MYP Certificate requires satisfactory completion of the programme's requirements including the Personal Project and, where it runs, eAssessment. It is not a prerequisite for Diploma entry at most schools, which means a family weighing effort between the Personal Project and preparation for the Diploma should ask their own school what the certificate is worth to them specifically rather than assume.

sections.heading: The Personal Project, stage by stage, and where help stops
paragraphs: The Personal Project is assessed against its own criteria covering planning, applying skills and reflecting, each carrying a level out of eight. The crucial fact, which students consistently refuse to believe, is that the product matters less than the documentation of how it came about. A student who builds something impressive and keeps a thin process journal will score below a student whose product is modest and whose planning, skill development and reflection are thoroughly evidenced.

That has a timing consequence. The process journal cannot be reconstructed at the end, and a journal written retrospectively in one weekend reads exactly like one written retrospectively in one weekend. The highest-value intervention in the whole project is a single session near the start about how to keep the journal usefully: what to record, how often, and what counts as evidence of a skill being developed rather than merely used.

The second highest-value intervention is at the proposal stage, testing whether the chosen project can actually generate development. A project that applies a skill the student already has produces nothing to document under applying skills. A project with no identifiable success criteria produces nothing to reflect against. Both are fixable in an hour at the start and effectively unfixable in April.

The boundary is tighter here than anywhere else in the Middle Years Programme, because the project is the student's own by design. A tutor may explain what each criterion rewards, discuss whether a proposal can generate real development, demonstrate what a well-kept journal looks like using an entirely different project, and read the student's own journal and report and ask questions. A tutor may not choose the project, make the product, write or rewrite the report, or construct the journal. The student is the person a malpractice finding falls on.

sections.heading: Standard or extended mathematics, and the Diploma consequence
paragraphs: This is the MYP decision with the longest reach and the least discussion. In MYP 4 and 5 mathematics splits into standard and extended, and the split is not merely about pace. Extended mathematics covers additional content and, more importantly, demands the algebraic fluency that the Diploma's Analysis and Approaches course assumes from the first week. A student who takes standard mathematics and then chooses Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level arrives with a gap that is visible in the first term and expensive to close then.

The honest mapping is roughly this. Extended mathematics keeps every Diploma route open, including Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level. Standard mathematics is a comfortable route into Applications and Interpretation at either level and into Analysis and Approaches at Standard Level with some bridging. Standard mathematics into Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is possible and is a genuinely hard first year, and families should go into it knowingly rather than discover it in October of DP1.

The criterion to watch is investigating patterns. A student who scores well on knowing and understanding and poorly on investigating patterns is fluent at procedures and weak at generalisation, which is precisely the skill the extended route and then Analysis and Approaches both demand. That pattern, visible in MYP 3, is a more reliable signal than any overall grade, and it is actionable: generalisation can be taught, and four to six sessions on it in MYP 3 or 4 changes what is available later.

For a family in Nad Al Hamar whose child is already in MYP 5 with standard mathematics and Diploma ambitions in a quantitative subject, the practical answer is the summer bridge. Six to eight weeks on algebraic manipulation, function notation and trigonometric identities before DP1 begins is the cheapest version of this problem, and it is far cheaper than a term of remediation in the autumn alongside five other new subjects.

sections.heading: MYP into the Diploma, subject by subject
paragraphs: The transition is not uniform across subjects, and knowing where the steps are tells a family where to spend. Mathematics has the largest step, because of the algebraic fluency question and because Diploma papers reward precise answers where MYP rewarded process. The sciences have a moderate step: MYP students arrive with better investigation instincts than IGCSE students, thanks to criteria B and C, and with less quantitative practice.

Language and literature has a smaller step than expected, because the analytical habits MYP builds transfer well, though the volume and the formality of Diploma writing increase sharply. Individuals and societies transitions well for the same reason: thinking critically in MYP is the direct ancestor of Diploma essay evaluation marks. Language acquisition depends entirely on phase reached, and a student in a lower phase choosing a Diploma language B course at Higher Level should check that mapping with the school rather than assume.

The step that catches almost everyone is the sheer volume of independent long-form work. MYP produces one Personal Project across a year; the Diploma produces an Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay and exhibition, and an internal assessment in every subject, most of them clustered in DP2. A student who found the Personal Project difficult to organise will find that cluster much harder, and that is the single most useful predictive signal a parent has.

Which suggests the best use of MYP 5 and the summer following it. Not content coverage, which the Diploma will teach anyway, but the two things it assumes: algebraic fluency and the ability to plan, draft and finish an extended piece of work without being chased. Both are teachable, both take weeks rather than terms, and both are cheaper now than in DP2.

sections.heading: Scheduling for a younger student in Nad Al Hamar
paragraphs: MYP students are between eleven and sixteen, which changes the scheduling arithmetic considerably compared with a Diploma candidate. They come home from the Mirdif and Festival City schools between about 3.50pm and 4.35pm, and the useful window is earlier and shorter than a sixteen-year-old's. A forty-five minute session at 5pm or 5.30pm achieves more than a sixty-minute session at 7pm, and attention rather than content is the binding constraint.

Frequency also works differently. For a younger MYP student, two short sessions a week beat one long one for almost everything, because the habits being built, justifying an answer, recording a process, structuring a piece of writing, are habits rather than knowledge. For MYP 4 and 5 students the pattern moves closer to the Diploma shape, with sixty minutes once a week and ninety when a piece of work needs reading and discussing.

The amount is also smaller than families expect. An MYP student who is coping does not need tutoring, and a tutor who says so is giving better value than one who proposes a programme. The genuinely useful purchases in this programme are narrow: four to six sessions on one criterion, a handful of sessions spread across the Personal Project year, and the summer bridge. Continuous weekly support across five years is rarely the right answer and is a large amount of money.

Ramadan shortens school days and brings door times forward by an hour or more, which for a younger student actually opens up a good early-afternoon slot. Families generally choose either that or a post-Iftar session for older MYP students, and both work over video in a way they would not with a tutor crossing the eastern suburbs at Iftar. Agree the pattern before the month rather than improvising in week two.

sections.heading: What MYP support costs, and when not to buy it
paragraphs: MYP tutoring sits at the lower end of the market because the content is less specialised than Diploma work, and families should take advantage of that rather than paying Diploma rates. Budget online platforms advertise from roughly AED 33 to 65 an hour, with Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52 and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65, and for criterion habit work with a younger student that band can be entirely adequate. A qualified subject tutor online is quoted at AED 150 to 300, with Unitors publishing IGCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200.

Where the higher band earns its place in MYP is narrow: the standard-or-extended mathematics decision, the Personal Project proposal and journal, and the summer bridge into Diploma mathematics. Those three benefit from somebody who knows what comes next, and somebody who does not will give advice that sounds reasonable and points the wrong way. For everything else in the programme, a competent generalist at a lower rate is the sensible purchase.

Bestimate's monthly estimates for a weekly one-hour arrangement run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end and AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle, and an online package of about AED 799 a month for eight sessions suits the twice-weekly short-session pattern that younger students need. In-home visits in Dubai are quoted at AED 180 to 500 an hour once travel is absorbed, which for MYP work is a large premium on a session that could be forty-five minutes on a screen.

The honest advice is to buy less than you were planning to. An MYP student who is coping needs nothing. One with an uneven criterion pattern needs four to six sessions on the weak criterion. One in MYP 5 needs a handful spread across the Personal Project year. One heading into Diploma mathematics from the standard route needs the summer bridge. That is a small total across five years, and a provider proposing continuous weekly support throughout the programme is selling a subscription rather than solving a problem.
