sections.heading: Approaches to Learning: the skills the programme assesses directly
paragraphs: Approaches to Learning is the part of MYP most often described to parents in general terms and most useful when taken literally. There are five skill categories, and several of them map straight onto criteria that carry marks, which means they are not soft extras but assessed content.

Communication covers reading, writing, speaking and listening, and it is where the communicating criteria in mathematics and individuals and societies sit. Social skills cover collaboration, which matters in group tasks and interdisciplinary units. Self-management covers organisation, affective skills and reflection, which is the cluster that explains most underperformance in the early years. Research covers information literacy and media literacy, which the investigating criteria assess directly. Thinking covers critical thinking, creative thinking and transfer, which is what the thinking-critically criterion rewards.

The reason to name them precisely is that each one is teachable and each one is small. Information literacy, for instance, is a handful of specific moves: establishing who wrote a source and when, checking whether it is making a claim or reporting one, extracting what answers the question rather than what is interesting, and recording the reference at the moment of use rather than at the end. A student who has been taken through that four times does it. A student who has been told to research properly does not.

The table maps the categories onto where the marks appear. For a family on this island with one tutored hour available, it is the best available guide to which skill is worth that hour, because the answer is usually whichever one is being assessed across three subjects at once rather than whichever subject looks weakest.

sections.heading: eAssessment, where a school enters for it
paragraphs: Some continuum schools enter MYP 5 students for eAssessment, which leads to the IB MYP Certificate, and some do not. The first thing a family should establish is which, because it changes the final year substantially and because a tutor who assumes the wrong answer will prepare for the wrong thing.

Where it applies, the components split in two. Several subject groups, including language and literature, individuals and societies, mathematics, sciences and interdisciplinary learning, are assessed through on-screen examinations. Others, including language acquisition, arts, design, and physical and health education, are assessed through ePortfolios of the student's own work. The Personal Project is moderated alongside. Grades are reported on the same one to seven scale as internal MYP grades.

The on-screen examinations matter for tutoring because they are, for most continuum students, the first genuinely external timed component they have met. Five years of criterion marking on teacher-designed tasks, with drafting and feedback and often a second attempt, gives way to reading unfamiliar stimulus material cold, working to a clock, and producing a single attempt. That is not a content problem and it does not respond to content revision. It responds to timed practice, mark-allocation discipline and the habit of finishing.

The ePortfolio components are a different matter entirely, and the boundary has to be firm. The work in a portfolio is the student's own, built over time, and a tutor can explain what the criteria reward and give feedback on what the student has produced. A tutor cannot make, write, redraft or supply any part of it, and nobody here will. That is worth stating plainly, because a portfolio assembled over months is exactly the kind of component where outsourcing is quietly offered elsewhere in this market.

sections.heading: The Personal Project, and the two failures that happen in week one
paragraphs: The Personal Project in MYP 5 is assessed on planning, applying skills and reflecting, each from zero to eight, with a process journal kept alongside whatever the student produces. Almost everything that goes wrong with it goes wrong in the first fortnight, which is also when a family is least likely to be thinking about it.

The first failure is a goal that cannot be evidenced. A student chooses something broad and admirable, then reaches the end unable to show what specifically was achieved or which skills were applied to achieve it. The applying-skills criterion has nothing concrete to point at, and the planning criterion suffers retrospectively because the plan was never specific enough to assess. This is entirely preventable by being asked three or four awkward questions at the start: what exactly will exist at the end, how will anyone know you made it, and which skill did you not have before.

The second failure is a process journal written retrospectively. A journal reconstructed over a weekend from memory is visible to any experienced reader, and it makes the reflecting criterion very difficult to score well, because reflection is about what was noticed at the time. The fix is a weekly habit of three sentences rather than an eventual essay, and that is exactly the kind of thing a short recurring session is good at maintaining and a single long session cannot.

The boundary on help has to be stated and not softened. A tutor questions the goal, explains what each of the three criteria rewards, asks what went into the journal this week, and reads a reflection the student has written. A tutor does not write, draft, redraft or supply any part of the project, the report or the journal. Submitting work that is not the student's own is a malpractice risk that falls on the student, and at least one operator appearing in these searches sells completed assessed work outright, which should be read as a warning about the market rather than an option within it.

sections.heading: The mandatory UAE subjects sitting inside an MYP week
paragraphs: An MYP timetable in Dubai is fuller than eight subject groups suggests, and a family adding tutored hours should know what else is on it. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and KHDA required these arrangements to be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year begins in April.

The requirements are specific rather than general. KHDA requires separate classes by group: for Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited because of the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. Standard Arabic is required as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, with the school's licensed-curriculum language used for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in Moral, Social and Cultural studies.

Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit, schools may vary lesson length provided the total weekly time is met, and KHDA advises that any mandatory subject lesson should run at least 25 minutes. Schools are also required to ensure that teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic hold appropriate KHDA approval for those subjects. And the use of different or additional content without prior Ministry of Education permission is not permitted, which places a real limit on how any tutoring in those subjects can honestly be described: supporting a student with the school's own material is a different offer from supplying alternative content.

For a Pearl Jumeira family the conclusion is arithmetic rather than regulatory. Eight MYP subject groups, the mandatory subjects, an activity programme from four until six, and in MYP 5 the Personal Project, all inside a week that ends at 3:30pm with a causeway crossing attached. That is why this page recommends one targeted session rather than a package, and why for younger students it recommends forty-five minutes early rather than an hour late.

sections.heading: Subject choices in MYP 5 that shape the Diploma
paragraphs: The decisions made in MYP 5 are the part of the programme with the longest consequence, and they are frequently made on the basis of which subjects a student has enjoyed most, which is a reasonable input and a poor sole criterion.

The Diploma requires six subjects across the subject groups, three at Higher Level, and several Higher Level routes assume performance in the corresponding MYP subject group. Mathematics is the clearest case, because the Diploma splits into Analysis and Approaches and Applications and Interpretation and several competitive quantitative degree courses specify Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level. A student whose MYP strength was investigating patterns and real-life application may be better served by Applications and Interpretation, and that is a decision worth making deliberately rather than by default.

The sciences follow a similar logic. A student strong on the inquiring-and-designing criterion is well placed for the Diploma's scientific investigation, which is 20 per cent of a science grade. A student weaker on processing and evaluating will find that same component harder, and that is useful information a year in advance rather than a surprise in Year 12. Chemistry at Higher Level deserves separate thought, because medicine and dentistry pathways generally require it and it is among the tightest tutoring supply points in Dubai.

What a tutor can honestly contribute here is evidence and workload realism, not a recommendation dressed as a requirement. The evidence is the student's own criterion marks across five years, read as a pattern. The workload realism is what six Diploma subjects plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and service actually looks like in a week that already loses an hour to the school run. The actual entry requirements belong to the universities, and they should be read on their own admissions pages before any subject form is signed.

sections.heading: Fitting an MYP session into the island afternoon
paragraphs: Age changes the timetable arithmetic, and most tutoring pages ignore it. A Diploma student can use a 7:30pm slot. An MYP 2 student frequently cannot, and buying an hour at that time produces agreement rather than learning.

The sequence here is fixed. Schools in the Jumeirah, Al Safa and Umm Suqeim cluster end between about 2:45pm and 3:30pm. The drive home means crossing Al Wasl Road or Jumeirah Beach Road and then joining the single causeway queue onto Pearl Jumeira, which takes thirty to forty-five minutes at that hour. Activity programmes occupy roughly 4pm to 6pm for most students. What remains for a younger student is an early window from about 4:45pm on activity-free days, and a short evening window from 6:30pm.

The practical recommendation for MYP 1 to 3 is an earlier, shorter session rather than a later, longer one. Forty-five focused minutes at 4:45pm will produce a rewritten paragraph or a properly structured plan. An hour at 7:45pm will produce a conversation in which the student agrees that the paragraph could be better. For MYP 4 and 5 a full hour works in either window, and in the final year a second session may be justified by the Personal Project and eAssessment arriving together.

One scheduling point applies across both groups. Activity programmes, school clubs and fixtures fill the calendar progressively through the year, and by January the available windows on this island have usually narrowed to after 6:30pm. Choosing the slot in September costs nothing and keeps the better one, which at this age is worth more than it would be for an older student.

sections.heading: What MYP support costs, and when it should stop
paragraphs: Published rates in this market, read in October 2026 and belonging to the providers named: in-home one-to-one tuition in Dubai at AED 180 to AED 500 an hour with travel included, with Bestimate's 2026 rate table putting the common range at AED 180 to AED 350. Online qualified subject tutors at AED 150 to AED 300, with Unitors listing IB rates from AED 200 and TutorChase AED 270 for specialist work. Budget online options from AED 33 to AED 52 at Tutopiya and AED 45 to AED 65 at EdFlik. None of these is an IB Gram price list.

For MYP the premium bands are harder to justify than at Diploma level, and that is worth saying rather than obscuring. The need in the early years is somebody who can read a criterion descriptor alongside a marked task and show a twelve-year-old what the band above requires. That is skilled work, it is not scarce work, and paying a travel premium for it on an island means paying for a causeway crossing rather than for expertise. In MYP 4 and 5, where subject content and eAssessment technique matter, the qualified subject band becomes the sensible place to be.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in Dubai or anywhere else in the UAE; in-home tutoring is a service offered only in India. Pearl Jumeira families are taught one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, which means the rate carries no travel and the descriptor and the student's own task can sit side by side on screen.

The last point is about stopping, which is the opposite of a sales argument and is the honest answer for most MYP families. An early-years intervention should last a term. Once a student starts tasks without being told, keeps a usable record, writes the reasoning without prompting, or proposes a specific improvement in an evaluation, the habit has formed and further paid hours buy reassurance rather than progress. In MYP 5 the hours are better redirected to the Personal Project process and the Diploma choices. No grade or criterion level can honestly be guaranteed, and anybody offering one has told you something about the rest of their claims.

process.title: Say which MYP year, first
process.description: MYP 1 to 3 and MYP 4 to 5 are different requests with different session lengths, different times of day and different market bands. Naming the year group before the subject prevents a family buying subject teaching for what is actually a self-management problem.

process.title: Send marked tasks rather than the report
process.description: Two or three returned tasks per subject with criterion marks written on them show which of four things is holding a grade down. Most families have this in a folder and have never read it as a pattern, and reading it is free.

process.title: Take the free trial lesson
process.description: A full session at no charge, taught rather than pitched, with the student. The tutor reads a marked task against the published descriptor and starts working. One trial lesson per student, before any booking; if the match is wrong, say so and nothing is owed.

process.title: Ask the school about eAssessment
process.description: Whether MYP 5 students are entered for on-screen examinations and ePortfolios changes the final year substantially. A tutor who assumes the wrong answer prepares for the wrong thing, and the school answers the question in one email.

process.title: Choose the slot for the age, not the convenience
process.description: For MYP 1 to 3 we recommend forty-five minutes at around 4:45pm over an hour after 7:30pm, and we will say when a requested time is too late to be worth paying for. The better window on this island is gone by January.

whyPoints.title: Two problems, told apart before anything is sold
whyPoints.description: Early-years MYP underperformance is usually self-management, research habits and criterion awareness. MYP 4 and 5 is content plus assessment technique. Selling the second arrangement for the first problem is the commonest waste in this part of the market.

whyPoints.title: Approaches to Learning taken literally
whyPoints.description: The five skill categories map onto criteria that carry marks, so they are assessed content rather than soft extras. Information literacy in particular is a handful of specific moves, and a student taken through them four times does them.

whyPoints.title: eAssessment treated as a timed-performance problem
whyPoints.description: On-screen examinations are the first external timed component most continuum students meet. Five years of drafting and feedback gives way to one attempt against a clock, and that responds to timed practice rather than to content revision.

whyPoints.title: Descriptors and work shown together
whyPoints.description: The fastest change in MYP comes from reading the band above aloud and rewriting one paragraph to meet it. Online delivery puts the descriptor and the student's own task in view at once, and the rewritten version is kept rather than lost.

whyPoints.title: Firm limits on the Personal Project and portfolios
whyPoints.description: A tutor questions the goal, explains the criteria and reads what the student has written. No part of a project, report, journal or ePortfolio is written, made, redrafted or supplied here, which matters most in exactly the components built over months.

whyPoints.title: An end point, named in advance
whyPoints.description: Most early-years MYP tutoring should last a term, and in MYP 5 the hours are better redirected than extended. No grade or criterion level is guaranteed, and the recommendation at the end of a term is sometimes to stop paying.

faqs.question: Does my MYP 2 child need a subject tutor or something else?
faqs.answer: Usually something else. In MYP 1 to 3 most underperformance is self-management and research habits rather than content: not starting until the evening before, keeping no record of what was done, treating the presentation of reasoning as optional. Those are three specific habits assessed directly through the criteria, and each takes a few weeks of being required rather than reminded. A student who knows the content and receives middling criterion marks is rarely short of knowledge.

faqs.question: How does MYP tutoring change between MYP 3 and MYP 4?
faqs.answer: Content starts to matter in its own right, because the subject groups are deepening towards Diploma level and gaps begin to compound. Session length moves from a productive forty-five minutes to a full hour. And in the final year three things arrive together: eAssessment where the school enters for it, the Personal Project, and the subject choices that shape the Diploma. That combination justifies a standing weekly booking in a way MYP 2 usually does not.

faqs.question: What are the Approaches to Learning skills, specifically?
faqs.answer: Five categories. Communication covers reading, writing, speaking and listening. Social covers collaboration. Self-management covers organisation, affective skills and reflection. Research covers information literacy and media literacy. Thinking covers critical thinking, creative thinking and transfer. Several map straight onto criteria that carry marks, which makes them assessed content rather than soft extras, and each is small enough to teach directly. That is why one hour on the weak category can lift grades in three subjects at once.

faqs.question: How do you actually teach research skill to an MYP student?
faqs.answer: As a sequence of specific moves rather than as advice. Establish who wrote the source and when. Check whether it is making a claim or reporting one. Extract what answers the question rather than what is interesting. Record the reference at the moment of use rather than at the end. A student taken through that four times with their own task in front of them does it thereafter. A student told to research properly does not, which is why the investigating criteria stay low.

faqs.question: Does my child's school enter MYP 5 students for eAssessment?
faqs.answer: Some continuum schools do and some do not, and it changes the final year substantially, so it is worth one email to the school. Where it applies, several subject groups including language and literature, individuals and societies, mathematics, sciences and interdisciplinary learning are assessed through on-screen examinations, while language acquisition, arts, design and physical and health education are assessed through ePortfolios. The Personal Project is moderated alongside, and grades are reported on the same one to seven scale.

faqs.question: Why are on-screen MYP examinations difficult for strong students?
faqs.answer: Because they are the first genuinely external timed component most continuum students have met. Five years of criterion marking on teacher-designed tasks, with drafting, feedback and often a second attempt, gives way to reading unfamiliar stimulus material cold, working to a clock and producing a single attempt. Content knowledge is rarely the issue. What is new is finishing, writing to the mark allocation rather than to the quality the student wants, and accepting one attempt.

faqs.question: Can a tutor work on an MYP ePortfolio with my child?
faqs.answer: Only on the criteria and on feedback. An ePortfolio is the student's own work, built over time, in language acquisition, arts, design or physical and health education. A tutor can explain what each criterion rewards and respond to what the student has produced. A tutor cannot make, write, redraft or supply any part of it, and nobody here will. That boundary matters most in exactly this kind of component, assembled over months, where outsourcing is quietly offered elsewhere in this market.

faqs.question: What goes wrong with the Personal Project in the first fortnight?
faqs.answer: Two things, and both are preventable. A goal so broad that nothing specific can be shown to have been achieved, which leaves the applying-skills criterion with nothing to point at and the planning criterion weak in retrospect. And a process journal that is not being kept, so it gets reconstructed from memory later, which any experienced reader can see and which makes the reflecting criterion very hard to score well. Three awkward questions at the start prevent both.

faqs.question: Which three questions should an MYP 5 student be asked about their project goal?
faqs.answer: What exactly will exist at the end of this. How will anyone be able to tell that you made it. And which skill did you not have before starting that you will have to acquire. A goal that survives those three is specific enough for the planning and applying-skills criteria to engage with. A goal that does not survive them will produce a project that feels successful to the student and scores poorly, which is the commonest and most avoidable disappointment in MYP 5.

faqs.question: How do the mandatory UAE subjects affect an MYP timetable?
faqs.answer: They add real load on top of eight subject groups. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum, with KHDA requiring implementation by the start of the 2025-26 academic year. Instructional time is calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit and KHDA advises at least 25 minutes per mandatory lesson. Schools must also organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in the relevant subjects, which is a specific scheduling requirement.

faqs.question: Can we get tutoring in Arabic or Islamic Education alongside MYP?
faqs.answer: Support with the school's own material, yes, and with a limitation worth knowing. KHDA requires that teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic in Dubai schools hold appropriate KHDA approval for those subjects, and for the mandatory subjects the use of different or additional content without prior Ministry of Education permission is not permitted. So helping a student with what the school is teaching is a different offer from supplying alternative material, and any provider describing it otherwise is overstating what can honestly be delivered.

faqs.question: How should MYP 5 subject choices for the Diploma be made?
faqs.answer: From the student's own criterion evidence across five years, plus the stated entry requirements of the courses they might plausibly apply for, read on the universities' own admissions pages. A student strong on investigating patterns is suited to abstraction and proof-style work; one strong on real-life application is often better served by Applications and Interpretation, which is a different course rather than an easier one. Workload realism matters too: six subjects plus the core is a full week.

faqs.question: What time should an MYP session run for a child on Pearl Jumeira?
faqs.answer: For MYP 1 to 3, around 4:45pm on an activity-free day, and forty-five minutes rather than an hour. School here ends between 2:45pm and 3:30pm and the Al Wasl Road crossing plus the causeway queue takes thirty to forty-five minutes, with activities to about 6pm. For MYP 4 and 5 a full hour works either early or from 6:45pm. For the younger years, forty-five focused minutes early beats an hour at 7:45pm, which produces agreement rather than learning.

faqs.question: How long should we keep paying for MYP tutoring?
faqs.answer: In the early years, a term. Once a student starts tasks without being told, keeps a usable record, writes the reasoning without prompting or proposes a specific improvement in an evaluation, the habit has formed and further hours buy reassurance rather than progress. In MYP 5 the hours are better redirected to the Personal Project process and the Diploma choices than extended. No grade or criterion level can honestly be guaranteed, and sometimes the right recommendation is to stop.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-pearl-jumeira.closingHeading: Name the year group, then the problem, then the slot
dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-pearl-jumeira.closingBody: MYP tutoring goes wrong when a family buys subject teaching for a self-management problem, or an hour at 7:45pm for a twelve-year-old. So the order matters. Say which MYP year the student is in. Pull two or three marked tasks per subject out of the folder and read the criterion marks as a pattern rather than the grades. Ask the school whether MYP 5 students are entered for eAssessment. Then pick a slot that suits the age rather than the diary. Take the free trial lesson first; teaching is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-remraam.tutorsIntro: These tutors work with Middle Years students across the subject groups most requested from this corridor. The first question is always which year the student is in, because a Year 7 criterion conversation and a Year 11 exit conversation are entirely different pieces of work.

intro.heading: A programme with no exams still has a calendar
paragraphs: The Middle Years Programme has no compulsory external examination, and that absence hides a timetable. Families who arrive from a British-curriculum primary expect pressure to build towards a date and find none, so the five years feel undifferentiated until something goes wrong in the final one. In fact each year decides something, and most of those decisions are easier to influence early than to repair late.

Year 7 decides whether a student learns the assessment language. Criterion descriptors, command terms and the expectation of reflection are all new, and a child who has not absorbed them by the end of that year spends the next four being marked on skills nobody has named for them. Years 8 and 9 decide habits: research, documentation, drafting and the willingness to justify rather than state. Year 10 begins to decide subject direction and, in several schools, standard against extended routes in mathematics.

Year 11 is dense. The Personal Project runs through it, service as action documentation has to be complete, interdisciplinary work continues, and in parallel a family is choosing what comes next: the IB Diploma, A Levels, or in some schools an IGCSE year. Any of those involves applications and in some cases interviews. A student arriving in Year 11 without the documentation habit from earlier years will spend it reconstructing evidence instead of producing work.

Remraam shapes the practical side. It is a low-rise apartment community in Dubailand, built as the Al Thamam and Al Ramth clusters with its own park and retail, reached from Al Qudra Road and Emirates Road. Middle Years provision here means travelling: the nearest continuum schools are Fairgreen International in The Sustainable City and GEMS International School Al Khail, with Nord Anglia International School Dubai further along Al Khail Road, while South View School and most local provision runs British curriculum.

One further feature of the programme makes the calendar harder to see than it should be. Because the school sets every internal deadline, two Middle Years students living in the same Remraam building but attending different schools can face reporting points, interdisciplinary units and Personal Project milestones months apart. Advice shared between neighbours is therefore less transferable here than in a British-curriculum community, and the only reliable source of dates is the school's own calendar, requested in writing at the start of each year.

That travel matters for a younger student more than for a Diploma one. A Year 8 home at half past five is not going to produce an alert hour at seven, and for this age group shorter and earlier sessions beat longer and later ones. Delivery is one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, which is what makes an early slot possible at all. Home visits are a service IB Gram runs in India only.

programmes.name: The eight subject groups
programmes.description: Each group assessed against four criteria labelled A to D, marked out of eight and converted to a 1 to 7 grade through published boundaries. Reporting happens on the school's own cycle, which makes those cycles the natural review points for any tutoring plan.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai the eight groups run alongside the mandatory UAE subjects, which every private school must teach whatever curriculum it is licensed for. programmes.name: The Personal Project, service as action and interdisciplinary units
programmes.description: At least one interdisciplinary unit each year with its own criteria, service as action documented throughout, and the Personal Project in the final year assessed on planning, applying skills, reflecting and the report rather than on the product.
programmes.countryNote: These are scheduled internally by the school, so their dates differ between the Dubai schools students from this corridor attend and cannot be found in a general guide. Asking for the school's own calendar at the start of each year is the single most useful administrative act available.

programmes.name: The Year 11 exit decision
programmes.description: After the final Middle Years year a student moves to the IB Diploma, to A Levels, or in some schools into an IGCSE year. Each destination expects something different, and MYP criterion marks are not directly comparable to IGCSE grades, which makes the conversation harder than it should be.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-remraam.subjectsIntro: These are the subject groups most requested from this corridor, with the year in which each one's characteristic difficulty usually appears.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Investigating patterns is the criterion that surprises families, because it rewards generalising, testing and justifying rather than reaching an answer. It usually becomes visible in Year 8 and matters for route placement by Year 10.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: Inquiring and designing, then processing and evaluating. Designing a method another person could follow is the skill that takes longest to build, and it is worth starting in Year 8 rather than Year 10.

subjects.name: Individuals and Societies
subjects.description: Thinking critically is where marks go: students describe sources where the descriptor asks them to evaluate reliability and perspective. This typically surfaces in Year 9 as work becomes source-based.

subjects.name: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Analysing is the under-served criterion, because students summarise what a text says rather than examining how it achieves its effect. The gap widens through Years 9 and 10 if nobody names it.

subjects.name: Language Acquisition
subjects.description: Assessed by phase rather than by year group, so a student can sit in different phases across the four skills. That mismatch confuses parents reading a single reported grade and is worth asking about directly.

subjects.name: Arabic
subjects.description: Taught both as a Middle Years language and as a KHDA-mandated subject, with separate classes required for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, so two sets of expectations can appear on one report.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: Marks sit in the design cycle documentation rather than in the artefact, which students find counter-intuitive and which makes it the best early training for the Personal Project journal.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.description: The process journal carries more weight than the finished piece. Students who treat it as an afterthought lose marks that cannot be recovered later, and the habit transfers directly to Year 11.

subjects.name: Physical and Health Education
subjects.description: Reflecting and improving performance is assessed, which makes written work part of a subject students assume is entirely practical. It is often the first place a reflection habit can be built painlessly.

sections.heading: The five-year arc and what each year decides
paragraphs: The Middle Years Programme is five years long and families treat it as one undifferentiated stretch, largely because nothing external punctuates it. Reading it as a sequence of decisions makes it far easier to support, and most of those decisions cost nothing to address early and a great deal to repair late.

Year 7 is about language, in the assessment sense. Criterion descriptors, command terms, reflection and the expectation that a piece of work demonstrates a skill rather than reproduces content are all new, and students arriving from a British primary have met none of them. A child who has absorbed that vocabulary by the end of Year 7 is set up; one who has not spends four years being marked against standards nobody has explained.

Years 8 and 9 build habits. The research habit, the documentation habit, the drafting habit and the willingness to justify rather than state are what the final years assume, and all four are cheaper to build at thirteen than at fifteen. Design and Arts are unusually good places to build the documentation habit, because their process journals are assessed and therefore give the habit a reason to exist.

Year 10 begins to decide direction: subject preferences, route placement in mathematics where a school runs standard and extended, and the shape of the exit conversation. Year 11 then carries the Personal Project, final documentation, continuing interdisciplinary work and an application process at the same time. Families who have treated Years 8 and 9 as a quiet period feel all of that arrive at once.

sections.heading: Reporting cycles, and when a criterion mark is actionable
paragraphs: Because there is no external examination, the school's reporting cycle is the only regular signal a family gets, and it is the natural rhythm for any tutoring plan. A plan reviewed monthly in a programme that reports twice or three times a year is reviewed against nothing; a plan reviewed at each reporting point has fresh evidence every time.

A criterion mark becomes actionable only when it is read beside the work that earned it and the descriptor the school applied. On its own it is a number out of eight whose meaning is exactly what is in question. With the marked task and the descriptor open together, the gap is almost always nameable in one sentence, and usually it is one verb: the work described where the next band asks for analysis, or applied a method without justifying the choice.

Reading across criteria rather than at one is the second step. A strong Criterion A with a weak Criterion D in sciences means the content is known and the reflection is not. The reverse pattern means something entirely different. Those two students need different help, and the single reported grade hides the difference, which is why the grade is the least useful part of a Middle Years report.

The third step is timing the response. One skill, practised before the next reporting point, is a realistic target. Four skills is not, and a plan aiming at four produces no visible movement and a disappointed family. Choosing the one skill with the largest gap and the clearest descriptor is the judgement a session is actually buying.

sections.heading: The Personal Project year, counted backwards
paragraphs: The Personal Project is the one Middle Years component with a shape families recognise, and it still goes wrong for calendar reasons rather than ability ones. It is assessed on planning, applying skills, reflecting and the report, not on how impressive the product is, and the evidence for three of those four accumulates while the work happens rather than afterwards.

Counting backwards from the submission date gives a usable plan. At the start of the year the goal is set, and a narrow specific goal produces rich evidence while an ambitious one produces thin evidence and a rushed journal. Within the first weeks the journal habit has to be running, because a journal written at the end is visibly different from one kept throughout and a supervisor can tell. The middle of the year is for the work itself, with journal entries dated as it proceeds. The final stretch is for the report, structured against the criteria.

The failure modes are predictable and all of them are early. A goal too broad to evidence. A goal requiring resources the student cannot access. No journal until the final term. And a report written as a description of what happened rather than as a response to the criteria. A single session interrogating the goal at the start of the year prevents the first two and makes the fourth much easier.

The boundary is strict. A tutor may explain each criterion, interrogate the goal until it is achievable and assessable, ask the questions the descriptors imply, suggest journal habits and give feedback on a report draft the student has written. A tutor may not plan the project, produce any part of the product, draft the report or write journal entries. The project is authenticated by the school.

sections.heading: Service as action, interdisciplinary units and the quiet deadlines
paragraphs: Two further elements run across the programme and both are documented rather than examined, which is precisely why they become a problem in the final year. Service as action continues throughout, with expectations that vary by school, and interdisciplinary units run at least annually with their own criteria.

Service as action catches families who have moved from a British-curriculum school, where nothing comparable exists. The expectation is not usually onerous in substance; it is onerous when four years of activity has to be recalled and evidenced in a few weeks. Recording as it happens, in the same place as the Personal Project journal later, removes the problem entirely and takes minutes a month.

Interdisciplinary units are assessed work and students treat them as a lighter project. The criteria reward integration between the subject groups involved rather than two separate pieces presented together, which is a specific skill and one worth explaining once rather than discovering through marks. Because they are internally scheduled they arrive without warning for a family that has not asked for the year's calendar.

The general principle for all of this is the same: in a programme with no external examination, the school's internal calendar is the real calendar, and it differs between the schools students from this corridor attend. Asking for it in writing at the start of each year is a five-minute action that prevents most Middle Years scheduling distress.

A practical suggestion that covers both elements at once: keep one dated log from Year 8 onwards, in whatever form the student will actually use, and record service activity and subject-project decisions in the same place. By Year 11 that log is already the habit the Personal Project journal requires, and nothing has to be reconstructed. It takes a few minutes a week and it is the cheapest piece of advice on this page.

Interdisciplinary units are assessed and reward integration, not two stapled pieces

sections.heading: The eAssessment decision and when it changes the final year
paragraphs: The Middle Years Programme offers optional external eAssessments, and whether a school enters students changes the shape of the final year substantially. Where a school does, students sit externally marked on-screen examinations and an ePortfolio in some subjects, producing a formal qualification at the end of the programme. Where a school does not, the final grades are internal.

The practical differences are three. The final year gains an external examination load in a programme that otherwise has none, which means a student meets timed on-screen assessment for the first time at sixteen. The student leaves with a qualification a receiving sixth form can read, which matters most for a family likely to change school or country. And revision becomes a real activity in a programme where it previously was not.

Because this is a school-level decision, it is a question for an open day or a parents' evening rather than something to assume. It also interacts with the exit decision: a student moving to an unfamiliar sixth form with an external qualification in hand is in a different position from one presenting criterion marks that the receiving school has to interpret.

Where a school does enter students, the useful tutoring adjustment is modest and specific: practice under on-screen timed conditions, which is unfamiliar to a cohort that has only produced coursework-style tasks. A handful of timed rehearsals removes most of the shock, and they belong in the term before rather than the fortnight before.
bullets: eAssessments are optional and the decision belongs to the school
Where entered, the final year gains an external load the programme otherwise lacks
A formal qualification matters most for families likely to change school or country
Timed on-screen rehearsals belong in the term before, not the fortnight before

sections.heading: The Year 11 exit, planned a year ahead
paragraphs: In Dubai the Middle Years exit has three realistic destinations and they expect different things, so the decision deserves a year rather than a term. A continuum school usually leads into the IB Diploma. A move to a British-curriculum school means A Levels, and because many of those schools run IGCSE in Years 10 and 11, a mid-phase move can mean entering an IGCSE year partway through.

The Diploma is the smoothest transition in assessment language: criteria, command terms, internal assessment and the expectation of justification all carry over, which is a genuine advantage. What does not carry over is examination load, since the Middle Years Programme has little or none and the Diploma is heavily examined. Students who have never sat a timed paper find the first mock a shock, and a few timed papers before Year 12 begins removes most of that.

A Levels are a larger change of kind: examined, narrow and content-dense, with a student arriving having covered less subject content and more skill development than classmates who did IGCSE. That is a real content gap in specific subjects and the summer before Year 12 is the right time to close it. Entering an IGCSE year mid-phase is harder again, because content order differs and tier decisions may already have been made for that cohort.

For a Remraam family the exit frequently means another school change, since MYP provision here already involves travel. Ask receiving schools three things a year ahead: what they expect from a Middle Years profile, whether they interview, and what bridging they recommend. Those answers shape both the final year and the summer.

sections.heading: A younger student's week, and the Dubai calendar
paragraphs: Middle Years students are younger than the Diploma students most tutoring advice is written for, and the practical consequences are real. Attention rather than content is usually the limiting factor, so shorter sessions beat longer ones, and two short sessions in a week often beat one long one because the practice is distributed.

Remraam adds travel. Middle Years provision in this part of Dubailand means a journey towards The Sustainable City, Dubai Hills or Al Barsha South, so a Year 8 can be home considerably later than a neighbour attending South View School. A session at seven with a tired twelve-year-old is not worth paying for, and saying so is more useful than filling the slot. Where the run is long, two shorter earlier sessions or a weekend slot usually works better.

The UAE calendar interrupts in the usual ways. During Ramadan school days shorten and energy patterns change, and because lessons arrive over live video with nobody driving, a slot can move after Iftar at no cost and be rearranged week by week. For this age group the sensible adjustment is shorter sessions rather than the same hour at a different time.

School breaks are the opposite case and are genuinely useful here, because the Middle Years Programme rarely sets holiday work. They are the only stretches with no competing homework, which makes them the natural window for a Personal Project push in Year 11 or for building a documentation habit in Years 8 and 9 without it feeling like an extra burden.
bullets: For this age, attention rather than content is usually the limiting factor
Two shorter sessions in a week often beat one long one

sections.heading: What Middle Years support costs, and the mandatory UAE subjects
paragraphs: Middle Years requests sit mostly in the qualified band rather than the specialist one, because the work is criterion decoding, habit building and project coaching rather than examination technique at Higher Level. A qualified subject tutor working online in Dubai sits at roughly AED 150 to 300 an hour, with Unitors publishing IB from AED 200 and IGCSE from AED 150.

Budget online and university-student tutors advertise from around AED 45 to 150, with EdFlik publishing AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya AED 33 to 52, which can be reasonable for straightforward homework support with a younger student and is less suited to criterion work, where somebody has to have read the descriptors and marked against them. Subject specialists run AED 200 to 450 and above, with TutorChase publishing AED 270. In-home visits are quoted at AED 180 to 500 with travel inside the price.

Monthly, Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 estimates for a weekly hour run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for 2026-27. These are market figures with their sources named, not IB Gram prices.

Alongside the eight subject groups sit the mandatory UAE subjects, which compete for the same evenings. Every Dubai private school teaches Arabic, Islamic Education and social and moral studies whatever curriculum it is licensed for, with KHDA's requirements implemented from the start of the 2025-26 academic year. KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, and combined classes are prohibited because curriculum expectations and the language of instruction differ.

sections.heading: Permits, boundaries and the questions to ask
paragraphs: An individual giving private lessons in the UAE needs the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18 and university students. MoHRE's own service listing shows no fees and a two-working-day completion time, and tutoring without the permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, with no published fine schedule.

A tutoring operation with premises and staff needs a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute instead, renewed annually with the request made at least 30 days before expiry. IB Gram has no UAE premises, holds no such permit, and does not use a regulator's name to describe its tutors. Abu Dhabi's professional-ethics rules also bar school staff from paid private tutoring of students enrolled at their own school.

On the Personal Project and on any assessed task, the work must be the student's own and is authenticated by the school. A tutor explains criteria, interrogates a goal, asks the questions descriptors imply, suggests journal habits and gives feedback on the student's own draft. A tutor does not plan the project, produce the product, draft the report or write journal entries. For the mandatory UAE subjects there is an additional constraint: the use of different or additional content without prior Ministry permission is prohibited, so support works with the school's own material.

The questions worth asking are specific to this programme. Have you taught the Middle Years Programme, in which subject group and at which year levels. Have you marked against the criteria. What will you refuse to do with a Personal Project. And do you hold the private tuition permit.

process.title: Say which year the student is in
process.description: Year 7 and Year 11 are different pieces of work entirely, and the years between decide habits rather than marks. Naming the year, the subject group and the school tells us which decision is actually live right now.

process.title: Ask the school for its internal calendar
process.description: Reporting dates, interdisciplinary units, Personal Project milestones and service as action expectations are all set internally and differ between schools. In a programme with no external examination, that calendar is the only real one.

process.title: Send the report and one marked task
process.description: The report gives criterion marks; the marked task shows why they were awarded. Together with the published descriptor they make a specific diagnosis possible in the first session, which numbers alone cannot.

process.title: Free trial lesson, descriptor open
process.description: A trial over live video at no cost and before payment, with the marked task and the descriptor side by side. The test afterwards is whether the student can say, in their own words, what the next band asks for.

process.title: Review at the next reporting point
process.description: Not monthly. The school's reporting cycle produces fresh criterion marks and fresh evidence, and one skill targeted per cycle is a realistic ambition. Four skills at once produces no visible movement and a disappointed family.

whyPoints.title: The invisible calendar is written down
whyPoints.description: A programme with no external examination still decides something every year, and most of those decisions are cheap to address early and expensive to repair late. Years 8 and 9 in particular are treated as quiet and are not.

whyPoints.title: Reporting cycles set the review rhythm
whyPoints.description: A plan reviewed monthly in a programme that reports two or three times a year is reviewed against nothing. Each reporting point brings fresh criterion marks and fresh marked work, which is what a review needs.

whyPoints.title: One skill per cycle, not four
whyPoints.description: Targeting the single criterion with the largest gap and the clearest descriptor produces visible movement. Attempting four produces none, and that judgement is most of what a session is actually buying.

whyPoints.title: The Personal Project is coached, never produced
whyPoints.description: Goal interrogation, journal habits, criterion explanation and feedback on the student's own draft are teaching. Planning the project, producing the product or drafting the report are not, and are refused. The school authenticates the work.

whyPoints.title: Sessions are sized for the age
whyPoints.description: Shorter and earlier beats longer and later for Years 7 to 9, and from Remraam the run to the continuum schools is long enough that this matters. A tired twelve-year-old at seven is not learning anything worth paying for.

whyPoints.title: The exit is planned a year ahead
whyPoints.description: Diploma, A Levels and an IGCSE year each expect something different, and a Remraam family choosing the MYP has often already accepted travel. Asking receiving schools a year early shapes both the final year and the summer.

faqs.question: If the MYP has no exams, what is there to plan around?
faqs.answer: The school's internal calendar, which is the real one. Reporting dates, interdisciplinary units, Personal Project milestones and service as action expectations are all set internally, so they differ between the Dubai schools students from this corridor attend and cannot be found in a general guide. Beyond that, each of the five years decides something: Year 7 whether the assessment language is learned, Years 8 and 9 the research and documentation habits, Year 10 subject direction, and Year 11 the project and the exit. Ask for the calendar in writing each September.

faqs.question: Which Middle Years year is most often neglected?
faqs.answer: Years 8 and 9, because nothing external punctuates them and the reports still look acceptable. They are where the research habit, the documentation habit, the drafting habit and the willingness to justify rather than state are built, and all four are what the final years assume. A student who reaches Year 11 without the documentation habit spends it reconstructing four years of evidence instead of producing work. Building those habits at thirteen costs a fraction of repairing them at fifteen.

faqs.question: How often should we review a Middle Years tutoring plan?
faqs.answer: At the school's reporting points rather than monthly. In a programme that reports two or three times a year, a monthly review has no new evidence to work from, so it becomes a conversation about effort. Each reporting point brings fresh criterion marks and fresh marked tasks, which is exactly what a review needs. Between points the sensible ambition is one skill, chosen as the criterion with the largest gap and the clearest descriptor. Four skills at once produces no visible movement.

faqs.question: Our Year 7 came home with marks we cannot interpret. Where do we start?
faqs.answer: With the marked task and the published descriptor open beside the report. A criterion mark out of eight is not a percentage; it describes what a piece of work demonstrated against a band, and the bands describe qualitatively different performance. With both documents in front of you the gap is usually nameable in one sentence and usually one verb: the work described where the next band asks for analysis, or applied a method without justifying the choice. Schools publish the descriptors and they are short.

faqs.question: When should the Personal Project goal be settled?
faqs.answer: At the start of the final year, before approval, because the goal decides almost everything that follows. A narrow, specific, properly resourced goal produces rich evidence across the planning, skills and reflection criteria; an ambitious one produces thin evidence and a rushed journal. Two of the four predictable failure modes, a goal too broad to evidence and a goal needing resources the student cannot access, both happen at that point. One session interrogating the goal then is worth several spent improving a report later.

faqs.question: Does the Personal Project journal really have to be kept throughout?
faqs.answer: Yes, and a supervisor can tell when it has not been. Three of the four assessed areas accumulate evidence while the work happens: planning, applying skills and reflecting. Dated entries recording decisions, difficulties and changes of direction are what the criteria reward, and a polished account assembled at the end reads differently from a working record. A student who writes three lines after each working session ends up with better evidence and less stress than one who writes an elegant narrative in the final weeks.

faqs.question: What is service as action and when does it become a problem?
faqs.answer: It runs throughout the programme, documented rather than graded in the way subjects are, with expectations that vary by school. It becomes a problem in the final year for families who have moved from a British-curriculum school where nothing comparable exists, because four years of activity then has to be recalled and evidenced in a few weeks. The substance is rarely onerous; the reconstruction is. Recording as it happens, in the same place the Personal Project journal will later live, takes minutes a month and removes the problem.

faqs.question: Are interdisciplinary units assessed, or are they a project?
faqs.answer: Assessed, against their own criteria, and at least one runs each year. Students treat them as a lighter exercise and then lose marks because the criteria reward integration between the subject groups involved rather than two separate pieces presented together. That is a specific skill worth explaining once rather than discovering through a mark. Because they are internally scheduled, they also arrive without warning for a family that has not asked for the year's calendar, which is another reason to request it.

faqs.question: Does our school enter students for the MYP eAssessments?
faqs.answer: That is a direct question for the school, and the answer changes the final year substantially. Where a school enters students, they sit externally marked on-screen examinations and an ePortfolio in some subjects, producing a formal qualification and adding an examination load the programme otherwise lacks. Where a school does not, the final grades are internal. It matters most for a family likely to change school or country, since a receiving sixth form can read a qualification without having to interpret criterion marks.

faqs.question: How early should we plan the move out of Year 11?
faqs.answer: A full year ahead. The three realistic destinations expect different things: the Diploma carries over the assessment language but adds an examination load the MYP never imposed; A Levels add specific subject content that IGCSE students have and MYP students have not; entering an IGCSE year mid-phase means a different content order and a tier decision that may already be made. For a Remraam family the exit often involves another school change, so ask receiving schools what they expect, whether they interview, and what bridging they recommend.

faqs.question: What bridging work helps an MYP student entering the IB Diploma?
faqs.answer: Timed papers, mainly. The assessment language carries over comfortably, which is a genuine advantage over students arriving from an unexamined background, but the Middle Years Programme has little or no external examination, so a student may reach Year 12 having never worked against a clock. A handful of timed papers in the summer before the Diploma starts removes most of the shock, and it is far cheaper than discovering the problem in the first mock. Subject content gaps are usually smaller than families fear.

faqs.question: How long should a session be for a Year 8 travelling from Remraam?
faqs.answer: Shorter than an hour, and earlier where possible, and we will say so even where it means a smaller booking. Middle Years provision here means a journey towards The Sustainable City, Dubai Hills or Al Barsha South, so a Year 8 can be home considerably later than a neighbour attending South View School. Forty focused minutes with the marked task open achieves more than sixty that drift, and two shorter sessions in a week often beat one long one because the practice is distributed.

faqs.question: What changes during Ramadan for a Middle Years student?
faqs.answer: For this age group, shorten the session rather than only moving it. School days are shorter and energy patterns change, and a child who would normally manage an hour will manage forty minutes well and sixty minutes badly. Because the lesson arrives over live video with nobody driving to Al Thamam or Al Ramth, a slot can move after Iftar at no cost and be rearranged week by week. School breaks work the other way and suit project or habit work, since the programme rarely sets holiday homework.

faqs.question: Do the mandatory UAE subjects affect a Middle Years plan?
faqs.answer: Mainly as competition for the same evenings, and as an extra set of reported outcomes. Every Dubai private school teaches Arabic, Islamic Education and social and moral studies whatever curriculum it is licensed for, with KHDA's requirements implemented from the start of the 2025-26 academic year, and KHDA requires separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs in Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies. Support in those subjects also has to work with the school's own material, since additional content needs prior Ministry permission.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-remraam.closingHeading: Ask for the calendar, then the report
dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-remraam.closingBody: In a programme with no external examination, the school's internal calendar is the real one, and asking for it in writing each September prevents most Middle Years scheduling distress. Then send the report, one marked task and the year the student is in, and a free trial lesson over live video is arranged before any payment is taken. The session should end with one skill named for the next reporting cycle rather than four. Lessons are online on Gulf Standard Time, sized for the age, and home visits are a service IB Gram runs in India only.

intro.heading: MYP in Serena means a long drive and a short evening
paragraphs: Serena sits off Al Qudra Road at the outer edge of the Dubailand belt, among clusters including Bella Casa and Casa Viva, with Mudon, Villanova and Remraam alongside. The belt is dense with British-curriculum schools and thin on IB provision, which has a specific consequence for Middle Years Programme families: most of them drive past several schools to reach an IB one, usually towards Al Barsha or the Sustainable City.

That makes the arrival time the first fact in any tutoring plan here. A student at Fairgreen International School in the Sustainable City can be home by 15:50. A student at one of the Al Barsha IB continuum schools arrives between 16:20 and 16:50, having spent forty to fifty-five minutes in a car after a full school day. Both students are commonly sold the same weekly hour, and only one of them can use it for demanding work.

The MYP compounds this, because its assessment is task-based rather than exercise-based. There are no past papers to work through in twenty-minute chunks. Instead there are investigations to design, data to process, texts to analyse and criteria to meet, and that kind of work needs an uninterrupted stretch when the student is alert. It is exactly the work that gets pushed to 21:00 and done badly.

IB Gram does not send tutors to UAE addresses — home visits are a service we run only in India — and there is no UAE office or centre. Serena students are taught one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, which makes the slot a scheduling decision rather than a constraint set by somebody's route. In a community where neighbours' arrival times differ by forty minutes, that is the most useful thing on offer.

This page therefore plans the week. Where MYP provision sits and what the commute costs. Which MYP work fits an early slot and which survives a late one. Why the homework pattern is lumpy and how to absorb it. How to carry eight subject groups without doing all of them badly. The Personal Project and the evening it genuinely needs. And what the criterion marks on a report should trigger.

Two standing notes. We publish no IB assessment or results dates, because ibo.org blocks automated verification; ask your school's MYP coordinator. And criterion descriptors are set by the IB and applied through each school's assessment policy, so your child's school is the authority on how a particular task was marked. For context on the market, Dubai's private sector runs 227 schools teaching 17 curricula to 387,441 students, with International Baccalaureate programmes at 7 per cent of enrolment, per Dubai Media Office figures for 2024-25. That share is why MYP provision is thin in this belt and why the commute, rather than the tutoring market, is usually the binding constraint on a Serena family's week.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-serena.programmesIntro: What the evening has to carry changes through the five MYP years, and the Personal Project year changes it most.

programmes.name: MYP Years 1 and 2
programmes.description: The years with the most spare evening capacity, which makes them the cheapest and easiest years to build habits in. Reading a task sheet before starting, writing in paragraphs that answer a question, and number fluency without a calculator. Sessions of forty-five minutes are usually better than sixty after a long bus journey.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai these years also carry KHDA-mandated Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside the eight MYP subject groups, with separate classes organised for Arabs and non-Arabs. For a non-Arab student that is genuine additional homework, and it competes for exactly the evening hours this page is about.

programmes.name: MYP Year 3
programmes.description: The year the workload steps up and the criteria start to bite. Investigation and design tasks in Sciences, pattern work in Mathematics and source evaluation in Individuals and Societies all arrive properly, and all three need an alert student. This is the year where slot placement starts to matter more than slot length.
programmes.countryNote: In many Dubai schools Year 9 is also when subject pathways begin to narrow and when families on an IB track decide whether to continue into the Diploma at the same school or move. A change of school at sixteen means a change of commute, which in this belt can be an hour's difference either way.

programmes.name: MYP Years 4 and 5
programmes.description: The Personal Project arrives, subject choices narrow, and in some schools eAssessment follows. Criterion marks begin to influence Diploma course placement, so a weak criterion in a subject the student wants at Higher Level has consequences beyond the report. The evening needs protecting deliberately in these two years.
programmes.countryNote: For Serena families this is also when the commute question becomes a school question. Several schools in the belt run to Year 11 and then expect a move for the Diploma, and the receiving school's expectations — which criterion marks it reads, in which subjects — are worth asking about early in MYP 4 rather than late in MYP 5.

programmes.name: The Personal Project
programmes.description: A goal, a product or outcome, a process journal and a report, supervised in school. It rewards documented planning and honest reflection rather than an impressive artefact, and it needs a regular small slot across months rather than a heroic fortnight. That makes it a scheduling problem as much as an academic one.
programmes.countryNote: The Personal Project runs alongside the mandatory UAE subjects and, in many Dubai schools, alongside IGCSE entries taken by other students in the same year group. Timetable pressure is the usual reason journals go unwritten until the end, which is exactly what the criteria are designed to detect.

dubai/ib-myp-tutor-in-serena.subjectsIntro: These are the eight subject groups with their criteria, plus a note on when in the evening each kind of task can realistically be done.

subjects.name: Sciences
subjects.description: Criteria A to D: knowing and understanding, inquiring and designing, processing and evaluating, and reflecting on the impacts of science. The design and processing tasks need an uninterrupted stretch and belong in the best slot available; content recall for Criterion A does not.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Criteria A to D: knowing and understanding, investigating patterns, communicating, and applying mathematics in real-life contexts. Criterion B asks for a pattern generalised and justified, which is thinking work rather than practice work and collapses in a tired student.

subjects.name: Language and literature
subjects.description: Analysing, organising, producing text and using language. Annotating a text for technique is the highest-value habit and can be done in a shorter late slot; sustained writing cannot, and should be moved to a weekend morning if the commute is long.

subjects.name: Language acquisition
subjects.description: Phase-based rather than year-based, assessed across listening, reading, speaking and writing. Speaking practice works in almost any slot because it is conversation; written accuracy work needs more attention and should go earlier.

subjects.name: Individuals and societies
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, investigating, communicating, and thinking critically. Criterion D is where most marks go missing, because critical thinking means evaluating sources and perspectives rather than asserting an opinion confidently.

subjects.name: Design
subjects.description: Inquiring and analysing, developing ideas, creating the solution and evaluating. The design cycle is the assessment, so research and specification work is as marked as the product. It is also the subject most likely to generate unpredictable evening load.

subjects.name: Arts
subjects.description: Knowing and understanding, developing skills, thinking creatively and responding. The process journal carries more weight than students expect: documented development can outscore a more polished final piece with nothing behind it.

subjects.name: Physical and health education
subjects.description: Knowing, planning for performance, applying and performing, and reflecting on performance. The written planning and reflection criteria are where academically strong students gain marks and where sporty students most often lose them.

subjects.name: Interdisciplinary units
subjects.description: Assessed separately on integrating disciplines and reflecting on that integration. Students treat them as double homework rather than as their own assessment, which is why marks here often sit below the same student's single-subject performance.

subjects.name: The Personal Project
subjects.description: Goal, product, process journal and report. Needs a small regular slot across months rather than a late surge, because the journal is the evidence base and cannot be reconstructed from memory in the final fortnight.

subjects.name: Approaches to learning skills
subjects.description: Research, communication, self-management, thinking and social skills, threaded through every criterion. Most MYP underperformance described by parents as laziness is a self-management gap, and in this belt it is often a scheduling gap wearing that costume.

subjects.name: Arabic and Islamic Education
subjects.description: Required by KHDA in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum, with separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs and combined classes prohibited. Real timetabled work and real homework, competing for the same evening as the eight subject groups.

sections.heading: Why MYP families in this belt drive further
paragraphs: The Dubailand belt is dominated by British-curriculum schools, and IB provision — particularly full continuum provision running the Primary Years Programme through the MYP to the Diploma — is concentrated elsewhere in the city, mostly around Al Barsha and Jumeirah South. Dubai's International Baccalaureate cohort is about 7 per cent of private-school enrolment against 37 per cent on UK curricula, per Dubai Media Office figures for 2024-25, so the geography is a straightforward consequence of market share.

For a Serena family that means two practical things. The school run is longer than their neighbours', typically forty to fifty-five minutes each way in the afternoon rather than fifteen to twenty-five. And the local pool of tutors who have actually taught the MYP, rather than taught a subject to an MYP student, is correspondingly thin, because tutors cluster where the students are.

The second point is the one that makes a proximity search unhelpful. There is no particular reason for an experienced MYP Sciences teacher to live at the outer edge of Dubailand, and plenty of reasons for them to live nearer the schools that teach the programme. A family filtering by travel radius is filtering by something unrelated to criterion knowledge, then choosing within whatever remains.

Removing the travel removes that filter. We match on the subject group and the criterion the marked work points at, and teach live online, one-to-one, with the slot set against your child's real arrival time. There is no IB Gram office or centre in the UAE and no home visits anywhere in the country, which is an India-only service — so the comparison this page makes is between an online specialist and the local in-home market, honestly stated.

sections.heading: Arrival times and which MYP work fits which slot
paragraphs: Here is the table that decides whether MYP tutoring works in this community. It maps the school clusters Serena children travel to onto arrival times, then names the MYP work that fits the hour that follows — which is the part no tutoring page bothers with.

The principle is specific to the MYP. Task-based work needs an uninterrupted stretch and an alert student: designing a fair investigation, generalising a pattern and justifying it, analysing a text properly, planning a design solution. Response-based work does not: marking a piece against a descriptor, annotating a text, labelling a diagram, writing a journal entry, planning what the next task will do differently.

That distinction matters more here than in an examination-based programme, because the MYP has no past papers. In IGCSE a tired student can still work through ten short questions usefully. In the MYP there is no equivalent filler, so a badly placed hour tends to produce nothing at all rather than something modest. Families often read that as the tutoring not working, when it is the slot.

For students on the Al Barsha run the practical consequence is a split week: the task work on a weekend morning, and a shorter weekday slot for marking against criteria and planning. It takes more arranging and it is the difference between a plan that lasts a year and one that lapses in February. Worth saying plainly to any provider: if the response to your arrival time is a fixed weekly hour offered regardless, that tells you how much thought the rest of the arrangement will get.

sections.heading: MYP homework is lumpy, and that is the scheduling problem
paragraphs: Parents moving from an examination-based system notice this within a term: MYP homework does not arrive in even nightly portions. It arrives as tasks with deadlines, and the tasks from eight subject groups do not coordinate with each other.

In practice that means a week with almost nothing, followed by a week carrying a science investigation write-up, a design specification, an extended piece of writing and an interdisciplinary unit, all due within days of each other. For a student with a fifty-minute commute, that second week is genuinely difficult, and it is where the term's marks are decided.

The response is not more tutoring. It is a calendar. Ask your child to put every task deadline from every subject group into one place — a wall planner, a shared calendar, anything visible — as soon as it is set. Nearly every MYP crisis we see in this belt is a student discovering on Sunday that three tasks are due on Tuesday, and nearly every one of those was avoidable a fortnight earlier.

Where a tutor helps is in the triage. Which of these four tasks carries the criterion the student is weakest in? Which one can be planned tonight and written at the weekend? Which needs the task sheet read properly before anything is started, because the criteria strands are listed on it? That is twenty minutes of a session and it is frequently the most valuable twenty minutes of the month.

sections.heading: A week that carries eight subject groups
paragraphs: Eight subject groups plus mandatory Arabic and Islamic Education cannot each have a dedicated evening, so the week has to be built on priorities rather than coverage. These are the priorities we would use for a Serena student on a long commute.

First, the subject group with the weakest criterion mark on the last report, because moving one criterion from a 3 to a 6 adds three marks to a total out of 32 and frequently crosses a grade boundary. Second, whichever task is next due in a subject that matters for the student's intended Diploma courses. Third, the Personal Project in MYP 5, which needs a small regular slot rather than an occasional large one.

Everything else runs on the student's own routine, and the routine is where a tutor can add structure cheaply: reading the task sheet before starting anything, keeping the deadline calendar current, and marking their own completed work against the descriptor before handing it in. That last habit is the single most transferable thing we teach in MYP sessions, and it costs no extra hours once established.

The table below sketches a workable week for a late-arriving student. It is deliberately light on tutored hours and heavy on placement, because in this community the constraint is the evening rather than the budget. A plan that asks for three tutored evenings from a student who gets home at 16:40 is a plan that will be abandoned.
